5. Can the authors comment on the following: With regards to the processing of the cryo-EM data,
I wonder if the authors also tested refining the other 3 classes obtained before proceeding with a
final NU-refinement of one of the classes. Considering the authors interpret their structure as an
intermediate conductive state, I wonder if there were some hints at other conformational states
captured in the data.
We tried refining the other 3 classes shown in the penultimate step of data processing pipeline,
but the resultant refined maps from these classes were of poor quality and offered no additional
new information. Hence, we went ahead with the map denoted as “class 0” for final refinement
and model building (Response Fig. 4)
Response Figure 4: NU-refinements of all the classes post 3D classification.
6. Could the authors comment why they mutated Y111H to mimic the corresponding TWIK-1
residue, but then mutated M135A instead of M135L (which would be the corresponding TWIK-1
residue)? What was the rationale/strategy here? And here again, it would have been ideal to have
TWIK-1 as a control experiment, and to compare Y111H with.
Methionine, leucine, and alanine are all hydrophobic nonpolar amino acids. Between M135L and
M135A, the alanine substitution of methionine reduces the size of the side chain drastically
affecting not only the size of the pocket near M135 but also affecting the relative hydrophobic
surface area. As we saw lipid-like densities around M135 amino acid, suspecting their role in
regulation of channel activity, we anticipated M135A mutation to have drastic effect on TWIK-2
activity compared to M135L. In the revised version of the manuscript, we also tested M135N to
explore the role of introduction of polar amino acid in this region on TWIK-2 activity. We notice
that both M135A and M135N mutants exhibit slightly slower channel activation and show no
drastic effect on the channel activity. However, M135A shows a greater loss of NPBA inhibition
compared to M135N suggesting that removing the bulky amino acid at this position affects the
efficacy of NPBA. Similarly, we also tested the effect of changing the pocket around Y111 on
TWIK-2 channel activity using a Y111A mutant. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while
Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type, like TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused
a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition. In the revised version of the manuscript, as per the reviewer’s
suggestion, we also compare pH-dependency of TWIK-1 in our assay set up and test the effect of
TWIK-1 like Y111H mutant on the pH-dependence of TWIK-2 channel activity. We find that
TWIK-1 is pH-dependent while TWIK-2 is not, despite the introduction of TWIK-1 like Y111H
mutation.
7. Could the authors comment/expand on the voltage-dependence of TWIK-2 in the, and whether
other K2P channels have also been found to be so.
In a 2016 study Schewe et al. provided significant insights into the voltage-dependent gating
mechanisms of K2P channel, challenging the traditional view that voltage-sensing channel
requires a canonical voltage-sensing domain. Instead, they proposed the SF to have a “check
valve” gating behavior. They also note that this type of voltage-dependency has been observed
in most K2Ps except TWIK113. Apart from the residues at the SF, voltage-dependent behavior in
K2Ps, especially the TREK family, is also regulated by other factors such as mechanical force,
ligands, and lipids 14–18. These reports suggest that the same K2P channel can switch between
voltage-dependent and voltage-independent current responses depending on their conditions,
perhaps a regulatory mechanism of certain K2P channels. Because we see that the central cavity
is occupied by lipid-like densities in our cryo-EM map, and because TWIK-2 has an ability to
translocate between endosomes and plasma membrane and has been proposed to interact with
other proteins via its C-terminus, we believe it is possible that voltage-dependency in TWIK-2
could be a context dependent phenomenon.
8. While I appreciate the modeling of potential lipids and co for the interpretation and figure
rendering of non-protein densities, considering the high ambiguity, I expect that the authors have
no intention of including it in the to be deposited model. (in the era of AlphaFold and machine
learning, everything that is deposited can and will be use by AI or others)
Compared to other K2Ps, the extra non-protein densities of TWIK-2 are a unique feature and may
be endogenous molecules involved in channel regulation. As noted in the manuscript, we have
not verified the exact nature of these lipid-like molecules, and hence we have modeled
hydrocarbon tails in these densities. While this manuscript was under revision, two other groups
reported structures of TWIK-2, and both groups observed tubular “non-protein” densities,
especially in the fenestration site and in the central cavity 7,8. The former modeled acyl chains in
the fenestration sites, while in the latter manuscript, the authors modeled lipids in these densities
and proposed a mechanism of lipid-mediated regulation of TWIK-2 channel activity. Encouraged
by multiple groups, independently, discovering lipid-like tubular densities in TWIK-2, we have
decided to deposit the model with hydrocarbon chains modeled into these densities.

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. However, the unique architecture of K2P channels
allows detergent micelles to occupy grooves formed between various secondary structure

interfering with refinement, we had to use a relatively tight mask to reconstruct a map with
interpretable features at the protein-micelle interface. We have tried to dilate the mask more, and
the resulting structure could not reach as high a resolution as the current map. A relatively tight
mask is needed to effectively remove the micelle density that is tightly bound to our protein.

Response to reviewer comments
We thank all the reviewers for their critical assessment of our manuscript. Our point-by-point
response is below. For purposes of clarity, we have reviewer comments in red italics.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
“This study determines a TWIK2 cryoEM structure and uses a commercial automated patch clamp
setup to assess the function of TWIK2 channel mutants and pharmacology. The structure of
TWIK2 had not been previously determined and this study provides a first look at the TWIK2
channel architecture. To accompany the structure, the authors perform electrophysiological
recordings of TWIK2, a channel that has been notoriously difficult (though not impossible) to
record from. Overall, the methodology in the structural and functional work appears to be sound
and the writing is clear. “
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the overall positive feedback.
“There are novel observations and interesting results in the manuscript but an informative
connection between knowledge learned from the TWIK2 structure and the functional studies
performed is largely lacking. The Y111H designed to mimic the TWIK1 pH sensing histidine and
the S4 site threonine residues are all positions that did not require a cryoEM structure to be
interesting candidates for mutation. While the M135A mutation is a candidate site based on the
TWIK2 structure, it is unclear why the authors chose this position as it does not occlude the pore
or play any clearly observable role in the TWIK2 structure. The experiments examining the effects
of ML365 and NPBA are interesting but somewhat superficial, as the mutants show some effects
on channel pharmacology but do not yield any substantive insight into where the drugs might bind
or how they might act.”
We thank the reviewer for pointing out weaknesses in this manuscript that could be improved. We
agree with the reviewer that the mutant selection was sparse. To address this, the analysis in the
revised version of the manuscript includes the following single and double mutants: F98A, Y111H,
Y111A, T106A, T214A, S213A, M135N, M135A, and T106A-T214A, focusing on the regions near
the SF, the K2P modulator pocket (F98A), and the hydrophobic cuff (M135A and M135N). The
alanine substitution of M135 (M135A) drastically reduces the size of the side chain, affecting not
only the size of the pocket near M135 but also the relative hydrophobic surface area. As we
observed lipid-like densities around the M135 amino acid, suggesting their role in regulating
channel activity, we anticipated that the M135A mutation would have a drastic effect on TWIK-2
activity. In the revised manuscript, we also tested M135N to explore the role of introducing a polar
amino acid in this region on TWIK-2 activity. We observe that both M135A and M135N mutants
exhibit slightly slower channel activation, with no drastic effect on channel activity. However,
M135A shows a greater loss of NPBA inhibition compared to M135N, suggesting that removing
the bulky amino acid at this position affects the efficacy of NPBA. Similarly, we also tested the
effect of changing the pocket around Y111 on TWIK-2 channel activity using a Y111A mutant. We
found that Y111A was slow deactivating while Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type
TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition, highlighting the role
of Y111 in maintaining SF1-M2 loop integrity.
To study the binding modes of ML365 and NPBA, we collected and analyzed cryo-EM data using
TWIK-2 complexed with ML365 and NPBA. We observed that in the presence of these ligands,
the sample appeared to be more heterogeneous, resulting in maps of lower quality compared to
the apo TWIK-2 map reported in this manuscript. The resolutions of both the inhibitor-bound
TWIK-2 maps are fairly similar (~ 4 Å), with one common feature being the loss of strong tubular
lipid-like densities that we observed in apo-TWIK-2 near the hydrophobic cuff. Of course, it is
possible that loss of tubular lipid-like densities is a factor of poor resolution of the map. To make
reasonable comparisons, we filtered the apo-TWIK-2 map to 4Å (Response Fig. 1).
Response Figure 1: cryo-EM map comparison of TWIK-2 Apo, TWIK-2 ML365 and TWIK-2 NPBA.
Two bottom views on the right indicate the occupancy of the cavity close to the selectivity filter (top)
and cytoplasmic site (bottom).
While we do not see any additional non-protein density in the ML365 dataset, we do observe
some non-protein density immediately below the SF in the case of the NPBA dataset. The non-
protein density that we see in the NPBA dataset is not seen in the apo TWIK-2; however, the poor
resolution of the map, and the size and shape of the density, preclude us from unambiguously
modeling NPBA at this site. Hence, we have not included these efforts in the manuscript and are
presenting them here in the rebuttal. As the efforts to obtain high-resolution inhibitor-bound
structures were not successful, we employed site-directed mutagenesis to identify a potential
NPBA binding site by performing more mutations in the SF, K2P modulator pocket, and around
the hydrophobic cuff. We have discussed these in the main manuscript and our findings suggest

However, loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities around the hydrophobic cuff compared to apo

“1) In the section entitled “Ion conduction pore of TWIK2”, the authors suggest that the carbonyl
oxygens of selectivity filter residues V107 and Y109 face away from the central permeation axis
in TWIK-2 and argue for the relevance of this SF orientation to TWIK2 function. Given the ~3.7
angstrom resolution of the overall structure, I cannot ascertain how the authors come to this
conclusion. Using the map and model provided by the authors, I can easily model the selectivity
filter within the map in a conventional orientation and find that I improve the number of residues
in favored orientations when the SF is modeled more conventionally.
If there is a biophysical argument to be made that the positioning of the valine and tyrosine
sidechains in the TWIK2 map somehow promote an unconventional SF backbone configuration,
this should be provided. Simply based on the map provided by the authors, I find this section to
be unsupported by experimental results. If the authors do feel their selectivity figure configuration
is accurate, a supplemental figure showing how the experimental map is better fit by the outward
rather than inward-facing carbonyls at V107 and Y109 would be extremely helpful to make the
authors' case on this point.”
We thank the reviewer for a thorough review of our structure. In our TWIK-2 structure, the SF has
been modeled with carbonyl oxygens of three amino acids – V107, Y109, and L217 – facing away
from the ion-conductance pore. While we agree that at ~ 3.7 Å resolution it could be challenging
to resolve the orientation of carbonyl oxygens in the dynamic loops of the SF region
unambiguously, we would like to highlight that the local resolution for this region is much better
than 3.5 Å (Supplementary Fig. S3F in the manuscript). As per the reviewer’s critique, we
attempted to model these three carbonyls in various combinations of them facing away or towards
the SF. However, just based on visually comparing the fits of these various models to density, it
is not straight forward to identity one particular combination of the carbonyl oxygens that fits better
to the map (see figures & table below). Hence, based on a comparison of the model statistics
such as bond RMSDs, Ramachandran outliers, Rama-Z score, & CaBLAM outliers for the SF
region, and the overall model quality statistics for the whole protein, we believe that the model as
it has been presented in the manuscript is the best possible fit (Response Table 1 in this rebuttal).
In K2P channels, the two conserved threonines at the bottom of the selectivity filter (SF) are the
only amino acids within the SF that coordinate K+ ions through their side chains. All other amino
acids at the SF coordinate K+ ions through carbonyl oxygens. It has been shown by multiple
groups previously that reorientation of the carbonyl oxygens away from the SF is a means to
regulate K+ ion flow, including channel inhibition, in potassium channels. Using X-ray
crystallography and cryo-EM, several groups have shown that reorientation of carbonyl oxygens
away from the SF pore affects the K+ ion coordination at the SF as part of C-type or pH-mediated
inactivation of the channel in KcsA, Kv, and TWIK-11–4. The flipped carbonyls often co-existed
with reduced occupancy at the canonical K+ ion sites (S0-S4) in the SF. As noted in the
manuscript, our cryo-EM map allowed us to confidently model K+ ions in only three out of these
five sites. Similarly, MD simulations on the prototypical K+ channels like MthK and KcsA have
shown that reorientation of the carbonyl oxygen of the conserved valine at the SF is one of the
initial steps that promotes dissociation of K+ from the SF and allows the SF to adopt nonconducting
or inactivated states5,6. As pointed out by the reviewer, we had provided only a brief biophysical
explanation for non-canonical carbonyl positioning in the discussion in the original manuscript. To
address that, we have expanded on the explanation associated with flipped carbonyl observation,
by including examples of other eukaryotic K+ channels (TWIK-1, Kv, and Kir) and their prototypic
prokaryotic homologs (MthK and KcsA) where similar observations have been made, as a
separate section in the discussion, & added more references to this section.

“2) In Figure 2B, the pore radius profile shows a constriction of the pore at around 5A from the
cytoplasmic face of the channel. This cytoplasmic constriction does not seem to be discussed in
the manuscript. Is this constriction brought about by the lipids modeled in the structure? If so, is
this at all relevant to the function of TWIK2? If the authors believe that these lipid densities are
important to shaping the TWIK2 pore, then this pore radius plot is appropriate. If the relevance of
these lipids is unclear and could simply be an artifact of the protein purification process, it would
be better to omit the lipid densities when running HOLE (or include a second HOLE profile in the
absence of the lipids) to show the profile of just the TWIK2 protein.
It would also be appropriate to discuss the lipid densities present in the map in the results section
of the manuscript, rather than the discussion. This would be a good spot to do so.”
The pore radius plot in Fig. 2B was constructed using the TWIK-2 model with hydrocarbon tails
modeled into the tubular lipid-like densities. We have now edited Fig. 2B to show the pore radius
profile with and without the modeled lipid-like densities. We did not include any exogenous lipids
during the purification. So, we believe these tubular densities arise from the molecules that co-
purified with TWIK-2 from HEK293 GnTI- cells. Because we could not verify the exact nature of
these molecules, we have only modeled hydrocarbon tails in these densities and called them lipid-
like in the manuscript. The discussion on the lipid-like densities has now been moved to the results
section in the revised version of the manuscript, as per the reviewer’s suggestion. While this
manuscript was under revision, another group reported a preprint suggesting a potential lipid
mediated regulation of TWIK-2 channel activity. They argued that lipid molecules “plug” the
channel on the cytoplasmic side by occupying the central cavity and by physically obstructing the
passage of ions, rendering TWIK-2 inactive. They demonstrate that R257, an amino acid towards
the C-terminus that lies below the hydrophobic cuff, is crucial for this lipid binding in the central
cavity and that the R257A mutation increases the channel activity, suggesting that channel
activation is a result of lipid removal or repositioning in the central cavity. In our TWIK-2 structure,
we observe lipid-like densities in similar positions (central cavity and along the groove formed by
the PH2, M2, and M4 helices) as reported by Mondal et al7. However, these lipid-like densities do
not entirely obstruct the access to the central pore (Fig. 2). The observation of lipid-like density,
corroborated by a different group independently, suggests that these molecules are relevant to
the function. We have added a few lines discussing this preprint and its relevance in the context
of our structure to the discussion section of the revised manuscript.
“3) For the experiments where G/GMAX–V curves are calculated, it does not appear that the
recordings reach a steady state at 200 ms. The current is still rising for TWIK1 wt and this is even
more pronounced in the mutants that slow activation (Figure 3B). Is it possible that the differences
in V50 are artificial, since the maximal steady state current is reached at 200ms in some of the
mutants but not in all of them.”
We appreciate the reviewer’s concerns regarding the possible underestimation of steady-state
currents due to incomplete activation at the end of the 200-ms depolarizing pulse, especially in
slow-activating TWIK-2 mutants. To reinforce the validity of our conclusions regarding mutant-
induced shifts in voltage dependence, we performed a new analysis based on normalized tail
currents, which better reflect the relative conductance by capturing the instantaneous current
upon repolarization—thus minimizing the effects of kinetic differences in channel activation.
Specifically, we constructed revised G/GMAX–V curves using tail currents, enabling a more
accurate assessment of the voltage dependence of activation across all variants. From these
curves, we calculated the ΔV50 values, which provide a more reliable measure of the voltage shift
caused by each mutation. Importantly, this alternative approach produced similar V50 shifts as
previously reported, confirming that the observed differences are genuine and not artifacts,
reflecting fundamental changes in channel gating properties. These new results are now included
in the revised Supplementary Fig. 5 and discussed in the Results section. To enable a better
comparison of currents across TWIK-2 variants, we have also modified Fig. 3 to now display
whole-cell current traces and activation time constants for all the mutants that we tested.
“4) I think the manuscript would be greatly improved by a more direct comparison of the TWIK2
structure with the previously published TWIK1 structures. Does this TWIK2 structure look more
like the low pH or neutral pH TWIK2 structure? Are there clear differences in the positioning of
the cap or TM helices? The entire section of the results devoted to an overview of the TWIK2
channel could be redone as a more direct comparison between TWIK1 and TWIK2 and would
significantly increase interest.”
We agree with the reviewer that a comprehensive comparison of TWIK-2 with TWIK-1 could be a
beneficial addition to the manuscript. In our first version of the manuscript, we had presented a
comparison of TWIK-2 and TWIK-1 in Figs. 5B, C and Supplementary Fig. S4, focusing only on
the conformational changes in pore domains, SF, and M4 helix. As TWIK-2 is physiologically
unlike TWIK-1, for the sake of completeness, we have also included comparisons with other pH-
sensitive and lipid-regulated K2P channels. To make these comparisons more apparent, we have
reformatted and expanded the figures and text to include a separate comparison section of the
TWIK-2 and TWIK-1 structures in their entirety. In addition, we have also included the results from
whole-cell recordings studying the pH dependency of channel activity in TWIK-1 and the TWIK-
1-like Y111H mutant of TWIK-2. Interestingly, we find that the differences in the structure of TWIK-
2 are localized to the cap region when compared with the TWIK-1 structure at pH 7.5. When
compared with TWIK-1 at pH 5.5, the differences lie only in the SF region, specifically the SF1-
M2 linker that houses the pH-sensing amino acid H122 in TWIK-1. TWIK-2 has the cap region
that is similar to inactive TWIK-1, but has the SF loops positioned in a similar way as that of the
active TWIK-1, despite the residue Y111 in TWIK-2 (H122 in TWIK-1) adopting a unique ‘up’
conformation. These new observations have been discussed in the revised version of the
manuscript, alongside the TWIK-2 and TWIK-1 comparisons from the older version (Fig. 1, 5).
The comparison of TWIK-2 with other K2P channels has been reformatted into a separate figure
(Supplementary Figs. 4, 7).

2. - In figure 1 (and for nearly all electrophysiological traces shown in the manuscript),
recording traces are shown on a signal scale that reads “Normalized I”. It is unclear what

it would be helpful if the authors explicitly discuss whether normalization was applied using

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue related to the normalization of
electrophysiological traces. In the revised manuscript, all figures now display traces showing
actual absolute current values instead of normalized signals. This update allows for direct
comparison of current amplitudes across wild-type and mutant channels as well as non-
transfected controls. Additionally, we now include current density for each experimental condition
where appropriate, ensuring that differences in current amplitudes are not influenced by variations
in cell size. We believe these revisions significantly improve the clarity and transparency of our

3- Given that the C-terminally truncated TWIK construct was not used for structure of detailed

We agree with this reviewer’s observation that the data on C-terminally truncated TWIK-2 is not
informative, beyond suggesting that TWIK-2 devoid of C-terminus is unstable compared to WT.
In accordance, we have now removed the C-term truncation data of TWIK-2 from the revised
manuscript.
4 - Is it meaningful that the loop region between V75-P89 is unresolved in the cryo-EM structure?
In all other K2P structures, this loop is well resolved. Does this mean that the V75-P89 is dynamic
in TWIK2, suggestive of a functional role? Or is this just a limitation of the resolutions of this
TWIK2 structure compared to other K2P structures? Does 3D variability analysis in cryosparc
give any indication of what is going on in this loop region?
The loop V75-P89 is a part of the CH2-PH1 region that harbors two predicted glycosylation sites,
N79 and N85. We used HEK293 GnTI- cells, which lack N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase I
activity, for overexpression of TWIK-2. So, it is likely that glycosylation at these sites is essential
for stabilizing this loop, and without such glycosylation, this loop is flexible and hence poorly
resolved in the cryo-EM density map. Interestingly, TWIK-2 structures reported by a different
group recently also lacked this region 8. Despite using glycosylation-competent Expi293F cells
and achieving an overall higher resolution structure (~2.9 Å). Perhaps, in TWIK-2 this loop is more
dynamic than other K2Ps. Another group reported structures of TWIK-2 while this manuscript was
under revision 7. They too use glycosylation-capable Expi293F cells as Khanra et. al., but were
able to resolve the V75-P89 region in their cryo-EM map. Moreover, they find that amino acids
75-80 in this loop actually form a short helix called ‘ear helix’ that is unique to TWIK-2, proposed
to stabilize the TWIK-2 cap domain. As this loop region can also potentially interact with the
keystone inhibitor site and the K2P modulator pocket, we attempted to resolve this region using
3DVA and subsequent classification in cryoSPARC (Response Fig. 3). However, our attempts
were not successful.
5- The panel in Figure 3 showing the relative locations of T106, T214, M135, and Y111 is critically

reworking this figure to make it clearer. The inset boxes are distracting, as each one has a different
orientation relative to the main panel. Perhaps a clearly labeled “top view” showing the Y111
residues, “bottom view" showing the M135 residues, and a side view like shown in the left side of
Figure 3A would be sufficient for this.
We have modified the figure as per the reviewer’s suggestions.
- “Notably, TWIK-2 channels elicited outward potassium currents that increased with
depolarization (over +30 mV), suggesting voltage-dependent activation of TWIK-2” Isn’t this a
surprising result, given that prior recordings in symmetrical potassium have shown inward
rectification rather than outward rectification? Is there any methodologic explanation for this
difference in observed functional behavior?
While it may seem surprising at first, the voltage-dependent activation of TWIK-2 seen in our
recordings agrees with previous studies, especially those indicating that TWIK-2 is one of the
least inwardly rectifying members of the K2P family, that inactivates and has a potential role in
electrogenesis9–12. Compared to strongly rectifying K2P channels, such as TREK-1 or TASK-3,
TWIK-2 exhibits more linear or even outwardly biased I–V relationships under certain recording
conditions. Moreover, differences in rectification behavior—particularly outward currents at
depolarized potentials—can depend on the expression system (e.g., Xenopus oocytes versus
mammalian cells), ionic composition, and intracellular environment (e.g., Mg²⁺, polyamines, or
pH). In our experiments, outward currents at voltages above +30 mV are probably caused by a
combination of weak inherent rectification and the electrochemical driving force for K⁺ efflux under
symmetrical or nearly symmetrical K⁺ conditions, rather than unusual voltage-dependent gating.
To clarify this, we added a section in the discussion explaining how our findings align with the
known electrophysiological properties of TWIK-2 and reflect system-dependent variability rather
than an unexpected gating mechanism.
Response Figure 3: 3D variability analysis (3DVA) and subsequent classification to resolve V75-P89
loop. The region shaded in gray is a part of the supplementary figure 3 in the manuscript and has been
included here only for reference. Particles from the best cluster displaying all the features of TWIK-2 from
3DVA step was used to generate an ab initio initial reference (cyan box). Next, particles from all clusters
with robust cap domain features (red boxes) from the 3DVA step were pooled for clean up by heterogenous
refinement and ab initio jobs. The final map obtained after NU-refinement, using the ab-initio reference
generated from the best 3DVA cluster, resulted in a map with features and resolution that resembled the
map already presented in the manuscript.
- Reference 70 in the manuscript includes data that describe the effect of mutations at the S4 site
threonines in K2Ps. For nearly all K2Ps, these S4 site mutations cause a loss of voltage
dependance. It is therefore interesting that in TWIK2, the T106A and T214A mutants maintain
their voltage dependent gating. Is there any rationale for why this might be the case?
The reference 70 reports that in channels without a dedicated voltage-sensing domain, the SF
itself acts as a gate and sensor. They demonstrate that mutating the conserved threonines at the
SF to cysteines causes loss of voltage-dependent behavior. However, they also show that in
addition to just these mutations, voltage-dependent behavior is also regulated by other factors
such as mechanical force, ligands, and lipids13. Regulation of voltage-dependency of K2P
channels by these auxiliary factors, apart from the residues at SF, has been shown in several
K2P channels, especially the TREK family14–18. These reports suggest that the same K2P channel
can switch between voltage-dependent and voltage-independent current responses depending
on their conditions, perhaps a regulatory mechanism of certain K2P channels. T106A and T214A
mutants display a reduced-voltage dependency in our experiments, but not a complete loss of
voltage-dependency. Because we see that the central cavity is occupied by lipid-like densities in
our cryo-EM map, and because TWIK-2 has an ability to translocate between endosomes and
plasma membrane and has been proposed to interact with other proteins via its C-terminus, we
believe it is possible that voltage-dependency in TWIK-2 could be a context dependent
phenomenon, in addition to being regulated by the residues at the SF. However, identification of
all the factors in TWIK-2 that regulate its channel activity needs furthermore substantial efforts.
- “Mutations T106A and T214A disturb these networks of hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic
interactions that stabilize the base of the SF and make the channel less selective and more open
(Figure 3B-3F).” The functional experiments presented in this section use only a single ionic
composition and are not suited to adequately address ion selectivity. Please support with data or
omit this claim.
We agree with the reviewer that with only a single ionic composition, it is hard to address the ion
selectivity of TWIK-2. We have rephrased this statement and added the observations from T106A
and T214A double mutants’ whole cell recordings to this section. We find that the double mutants
display greater current density compared to single mutants and wild-type TWIK-2.
- Is the TWIK2 Y111H mutant pH sensitive like the TWIK1 channel? This seems like an obvious
experiment to try and would be informative to understanding differences between TWIK1 and
TWIK2 functions.
As already discovered by a few groups, H122 in TWIK-1 and H98 in TASK-3 although regarded
as major proton-sensing amino acids in the SF1-M2 loop, are not the only determinants of pH
sensitivity in K2P channels4,19–22. While the Y111H mutant of TWIK-2 is a TWIK-1-like mutation,
we did not anticipate that it would single-handedly change the pH sensitivity of TWIK-2. In the
revised version of the manuscript, we show that the pH dependency of channel activation and
activity of Y111H TWIK-2 is the same as that of wild-type like TWIK-2. Furthermore, we observe
that in our assay setup, TWIK-1 showed pH-dependent current changes, albeit mild. These
observations have been included in the revised version of the manuscript in a separate figure,
and the corresponding text has been modified accordingly.
- More methodological detail of the automated patch clamp technique would be helpful to
understand the experimental system. Are drugs applied to the intracellular face of the channel
(via syncropatch pipette) or extracellular via bath?
We appreciate the reviewer's request for clarification regarding the delivery of compounds in the
automated patch clamp system. To address this, we have expanded the Methods section to
include more detailed information about the experimental setup. Unless otherwise noted, all
compounds were applied extracellularly using an external addition protocol, following the standard
procedures for the SyncroPatch system. The SyncroPatch features a high-speed, multi-channel
pipetting robot that manages all liquid additions and removals during the experiments. This robot
can simultaneously add various external compounds—such as drugs, ligands, and chemicals—
to each of the 384 wells, enabling a large number of experiments to be conducted simultaneously.
Additionally, the robot performs quick and efficient solution exchanges in the wells. Although the
system permits compound delivery to the intracellular face via an intracellular exchange solution,
this study only examined the external application of pharmacological agents to aid in easier
application, better ability to perform cumulative concentration-response curves, and for clear pre-
and post-drug comparisons. This clarification has been added to the ‘Automated patch clamp
recordings’ section within the Materials and Methods, to improve reproducibility and transparency
in our data interpretation.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
“The manuscript of Ma et al, provides new insights into the modulation of the K2P channel TWIK-
2 using structural and electrophysiological data. The study provides the first cryo-EM structure of
the full-length TWIK-2 at 3.7Å resolution, which is accompanied by mutagenesis studies and the
use of a whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology workflow. The authors show that TWIK-2 is pH-
insensitive but slightly voltage-gated and suggest potential different binding modes or
mechanisms of inhibition in TWIK-2 for two of the four tested K2P modulators (ML365 and NPBA).
The work is well executed and well written. However, overall the study fall a bit short. The new
insights provided do not represent a big step forward in improving our understanding of how
TWIK-2 (and K2P channels in general) function and are regulated. The substance and depth of
the study could be/have been strengthened by more structure-guided mutagenesis studies, a
more robust comparison of their new automated electrophysiology setup, a better literature
comparison with (mutagenesis studies of) TWIK-1 and other K2P channels, or even more
structural data or structural analysis. While I understand that addressing them all might be out of
the scope of this study, the manuscript requires a bit more of depth. Specific suggestion would be
(major comments):”
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions to increase the depth of our
work. We have revised the manuscript accordingly and addressed the changes point-by-point in
our response below.
1. In total ‘only’ four residues are identified as different/interesting and tested. Namely M135A,
T106A, T214A and Y111H. What about other positions, e.g., around the cavity or along the ion
conductance pathway? Is everything else conserved? What about testing mutating the same sites
with other substitutes or using double and triple mutations to gain more insights? Compare in
more depth with TWIK-1 and other K2P channels.
We agree with the reviewer that the mutant selection was sparse. To address this, we have
included 4 more single mutants in the revised version of the manuscript, focusing on the regions
around the SF (S213A and Y111A), the K2P modulator pocket (F98A), and hydrophobic cuff
(M135N). Additionally, we also tested the effect of the T106A/T214A double mutant on TWIK-2
channel activity. We have also included an extensive comparison of TWIK-2 and TWIK-1,
especially the channel activity, inhibition, and differences in the structure. Lastly, we have
reformatted the existing comparison with other K2P channels to make it more apparent. Please
see the remaining rebuttal, the results, and the discussion sections for more details.
2. Most striking in this endeavor is the mutant Y111H. The authors show that in contrast to TWIK-
1, TWIK-2 is pH-insensitive, with the histidine in that position being the pH-sensing residue in
TWIK-1. While the authors go on and attempt to describe some of the differences observed for
TWIK-2-Y111H, they never actually tested if this mutant has become pH-sensitive. Considering
the overall conservation between TWIK-1 and TWIK-2 this would be expected and highly
interesting to test. Further, to test the importance of the tyrosine and decouple it from a pH sensor
position, a mutation to another residue, e.g. Y111A and Y111L would be interesting. Finally, the
fact that TWIK-2_Y111H mutant carries the pH sensor of TWIK-1 must be mentioned in all clarity
also in the results and discussion section and taking into account during interpretation.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of Y111H. H122 in TWIK-1, although
regarded as a major proton-sensing amino acid in the SF1-M2 loop, is not the only determinant
of pH4,20,22. While the Y111H mutant of TWIK-2 is a TWIK-1-like mutation, we did not anticipate
that it would single-handedly change the pH sensitivity of TWIK-2. In the revised version of the
manuscript, as per the reviewer’s suggestion, we also compare the pH-dependency of TWIK-1 in
our assay setup and test the effect of the TWIK-1-like Y111H mutant on the pH-dependence of
TWIK-2 channel activity. We find that TWIK-1 is pH-dependent while TWIK-2 is not, despite the
introduction of TWIK-1 like Y111H mutation. As per the reviewer’s suggestion, we also tested the
effect of changing the bulky Y111 to a smaller aliphatic amino acid as alanine, on TWIK-2 channel
activity. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while Y111H was slow activating, compared
to wild-type TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition.
Perhaps, to speculate, the role of Y111 in TWIK-2 is maintaining the SF1-M2 loop integrity to
facilitate allosteric coupling between the bottom and top of the SF.
3. I appreciate and highly welcome the high-throughput patch clamp workflow presented by the
authors. However, considering i) the discrepancies mentioned by the authors on
electrophysiology studies for TWIK-2 in the literature, and ii) the mentioned inconsistencies
between some of their electrophysiology data with that published before, the authors should do a
more thorough comparison. If possible, between methods conducted by themselves with the
same non-glycosylated constructs (conventional patch clamp and high-throughput patch clamp).
But perhaps more importantly, use TWIK-1 in their automated whole-cell patch clamp
electrophysiology setup, for which more robust recordings have been reported. This would allow
us to assess and compare TWIK-1 and TWIK-2 and the different workflows better.
We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. While we agree that not all experiments
performed using conventional patch clamp can be adopted to a high-throughput automated patch
clamp approach, screening of inhibitors and testing the relative change in channel activity upon
mutagenesis has been reliably demonstrated by several groups. As there are already reports that
compare high-throughput APC with conventional patch clamp techniques23–25, we prioritized to
compare between TWIK-1 and TWIK-2. Using the same expression construct background and
Syncropatch assay set up, we found that the overall TWIK-1 currents are comparable to TWIK-2.
However, we notice that TWIK-1, unlike TWIK-2, shows pH dependency, albeit only mild. We also
find that TWIK-1 is faster activating than TWIK-2 and is more susceptible to inhibition by ML365
and NPBA compared to TWIK-2. In addition to the comparison of electrophysiological properties
of TWIK-2 and TWIK-1, in the revised version of the manuscript, we also include a detailed
structure comparison at the end of the results section.
4. The slightly different impact found for two of the tested inhibitors makes the discussion a bit
ambiguous as to their potential different binding mode. I wonder if an attempt to solve an inhibitor-
bound structure would be in the scope of this study as the authors seem to be able to obtain
enough stable protein and the processing appears rather straightforward.
We agree with the reviewer that the structures of TWIK-2 with ML365 and NPBA could provide
more information about their mechanism of binding. We collected and analyzed cryo-EM datasets
of TWIK-2 with ML365 or NPBA. We observed that in the presence of these ligands, the sample
appeared to be more heterogeneous, resulting in maps of lower quality compared to the apo
TWIK-2 map reported in this manuscript. The resolutions of both the inhibitor-bound TWIK-2 maps
are fairly similar, with one common feature being the loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities that
we observed in apo-TWIK-2 near the hydrophobic cuff. Of course, it is possible that loss of tubular
lipid-like densities is a factor of poor resolution of the map. To make reasonable comparisons, we
filtered the apo-TWIK-2 map to ~4Å (Response Fig. 1 above in page 2 of this document).
While we do not see any additional non-protein density in the ML365 dataset, we do observe
some non-protein density immediately below the SF in the case of the NPBA dataset. The non-
protein density that we see in the NPBA dataset is not seen in the apo TWIK-2; however, the poor
resolution of the map, and the size and shape of the density, preclude us from modeling NPBA at
this site. Hence, we have not included these efforts in the manuscript and are presenting them
here in the rebuttal. As the efforts to obtain high-resolution inhibitor-bound structures were not
fruitful, we employed site-directed mutagenesis to identify a potential NPBA binding site by
performing more mutations in the SF, K2P modulator pocket, and around the hydrophobic cuff.
We have discussed these in the main manuscript, and our findings suggest that the potential
binding site for NPBA, as hinted by additional density in the map, could be below the SF. The
mutagenesis exploration still does not identify the site for ML365 unambiguously. However, loss
of strong tubular lipid-like densities around the hydrophobic cuff compared to apo TWIK-2 makes
us suspect that ML365, like NPBA could bind through the cavity, albeit interacting with different
residues compared to NPBA.
Other major comments:
5. Can the authors comment on the following: With regards to the processing of the cryo-EM data,
I wonder if the authors also tested refining the other 3 classes obtained before proceeding with a
final NU-refinement of one of the classes. Considering the authors interpret their structure as an
intermediate conductive state, I wonder if there were some hints at other conformational states
captured in the data.
We tried refining the other 3 classes shown in the penultimate step of data processing pipeline,
but the resultant refined maps from these classes were of poor quality and offered no additional
new information. Hence, we went ahead with the map denoted as “class 0” for final refinement
and model building (Response Fig. 4)
Response Figure 4: NU-refinements of all the classes post 3D classification.
6. Could the authors comment why they mutated Y111H to mimic the corresponding TWIK-1
residue, but then mutated M135A instead of M135L (which would be the corresponding TWIK-1
residue)? What was the rationale/strategy here? And here again, it would have been ideal to have
TWIK-1 as a control experiment, and to compare Y111H with.
Methionine, leucine, and alanine are all hydrophobic nonpolar amino acids. Between M135L and
M135A, the alanine substitution of methionine reduces the size of the side chain drastically
affecting not only the size of the pocket near M135 but also affecting the relative hydrophobic
surface area. As we saw lipid-like densities around M135 amino acid, suspecting their role in
regulation of channel activity, we anticipated M135A mutation to have drastic effect on TWIK-2
activity compared to M135L. In the revised version of the manuscript, we also tested M135N to
explore the role of introduction of polar amino acid in this region on TWIK-2 activity. We notice
that both M135A and M135N mutants exhibit slightly slower channel activation and show no
drastic effect on the channel activity. However, M135A shows a greater loss of NPBA inhibition
compared to M135N suggesting that removing the bulky amino acid at this position affects the
efficacy of NPBA. Similarly, we also tested the effect of changing the pocket around Y111 on
TWIK-2 channel activity using a Y111A mutant. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while
Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type, like TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused
a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition. In the revised version of the manuscript, as per the reviewer’s
suggestion, we also compare pH-dependency of TWIK-1 in our assay set up and test the effect of
TWIK-1 like Y111H mutant on the pH-dependence of TWIK-2 channel activity. We find that
TWIK-1 is pH-dependent while TWIK-2 is not, despite the introduction of TWIK-1 like Y111H
mutation.
7. Could the authors comment/expand on the voltage-dependence of TWIK-2 in the, and whether
other K2P channels have also been found to be so.
In a 2016 study Schewe et al. provided significant insights into the voltage-dependent gating
mechanisms of K2P channel, challenging the traditional view that voltage-sensing channel
requires a canonical voltage-sensing domain. Instead, they proposed the SF to have a “check
valve” gating behavior. They also note that this type of voltage-dependency has been observed
in most K2Ps except TWIK113. Apart from the residues at the SF, voltage-dependent behavior in
K2Ps, especially the TREK family, is also regulated by other factors such as mechanical force,
ligands, and lipids 14–18. These reports suggest that the same K2P channel can switch between
voltage-dependent and voltage-independent current responses depending on their conditions,
perhaps a regulatory mechanism of certain K2P channels. Because we see that the central cavity
is occupied by lipid-like densities in our cryo-EM map, and because TWIK-2 has an ability to
translocate between endosomes and plasma membrane and has been proposed to interact with
other proteins via its C-terminus, we believe it is possible that voltage-dependency in TWIK-2
could be a context dependent phenomenon.
8. While I appreciate the modeling of potential lipids and co for the interpretation and figure
rendering of non-protein densities, considering the high ambiguity, I expect that the authors have
no intention of including it in the to be deposited model. (in the era of AlphaFold and machine
learning, everything that is deposited can and will be use by AI or others)
Compared to other K2Ps, the extra non-protein densities of TWIK-2 are a unique feature and may
be endogenous molecules involved in channel regulation. As noted in the manuscript, we have
not verified the exact nature of these lipid-like molecules, and hence we have modeled
hydrocarbon tails in these densities. While this manuscript was under revision, two other groups
reported structures of TWIK-2, and both groups observed tubular “non-protein” densities,
especially in the fenestration site and in the central cavity 7,8. The former modeled acyl chains in
the fenestration sites, while in the latter manuscript, the authors modeled lipids in these densities
and proposed a mechanism of lipid-mediated regulation of TWIK-2 channel activity. Encouraged
by multiple groups, independently, discovering lipid-like tubular densities in TWIK-2, we have
decided to deposit the model with hydrocarbon chains modeled into these densities.
Minor comments:
- Page 4: "we identified key amino acids that differentiate TWIK-2 from TWIK-1 and other
members of the K2P family". From what I understood, only Y111 was a direct comparison with
TWIK-1, so I suggest toning down this sentence.
We thank the reviewer for the correction. We have rephrased it to “We identified key amino acids
that regulate TWIK2 channel activity”, as we have included functional analysis of more mutations
in the revised version of the manuscript.
- Could the authors add details of this inhibition experiment in the Methods section (e.g. how was
the small molecule screening set-up, quantity/volume of compound added, (pre-) incubation time,
etc.). Could the authors show a blank/control measurement with just DMSO to account for the
buffer?
We appreciate the reviewer's request for clarification regarding the delivery of compounds in the
automated patch clamp system and the experimental setup (see above comments to reviewer 1).
The SyncroPatch uses 384-well chips with micro-apertures, where negative pressure captures
individual cells and forms high-resistance seals. A robotic pipetting unit handles liquids
automatically, enabling parallel compound addition, quick solution changes, and precise
concentration control, which ensures reliable dose–response measurements. We have updated
the Methods section to include more details about the inhibition experiments. Importantly, we
clarify that the reference (control) buffer always contained the same DMSO concentration as the
compound solutions, accounting for any potential nonspecific effects of the solvent. As a result,
the vehicle condition was consistently included in all experiments, ensuring that the observed
effects are due to the test compounds.
- Methods section: Cloning and overexpression of recombinant TWIK-2: The text should say for
better clarity: "with an N-terminal Strep-tag-II, followed by a GFP tag and a HRV-3C protease site"
instead of "followed by an HRV-3C protease site and a GFP tag" as it is then later stated that 3C
cleavage results in removal of GFP tag.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have corrected it.
- As the authors mention in the main text the poor heterologous expression of TWIK channels,
could they indicate the yield they obtained from their experiments?
As mentioned in the introduction, poor heterologous expression of TWIK channels has been
reported by a few groups before us 9,12,26. We were able to obtain ~0.4 mg of protein from 1L of
HEK293 GnTI- cells, after the affinity purification step.
- Correct typo in: "Mutations T106A and T214A"
We have rephrased that sentence in the discussion.
Figures:
- Please update figure numbers so that they are cited in correct order as mentioned in the text.
E.g S2 should be called S1; swap order of Figure 4D and 4E
We have made sure that the figures are in the correct order.
- Figure S2F: could the authors explain the uV units on the y-axis of the FSEC curve
- Specify in main text and S2 figure legend which detergent was used for solubilization of ΔC-
TWIK-2
- For better clarity, keep one naming for each construct between figure and figure legends (e.g.
in figure S2: TWIK-2 is sometimes called WT or wild-type; or ΔC-TWIK-2 (C-ter 1-276) is called
c-ter 1-276, c-ter and del1-276). In general, could the authors fix all the inconsistencies in the
figure legend of S2: missing periods, having a mixture of (n=15) and ",n=15" etc.
As per the other reviewer’s suggestion, we removed the ΔC-TWIK-2 data from Supplementary
Fig. 2 and the legend associated with it in the revised version of the manuscript. We have fixed
all other inconsistencies.
- Figure 2A: could the authors improve the illustration so that the ion conduction pathway is clearer
to the reader?
We have remade this figure in current version of our manuscript.
- Figure S1: indicate the non-conserved M135 and Y111 residues on the sequence alignment
All the sites that have been mutated in this study, including M135 and Y111, have now been
highlighted in the sequence alignment figure in the current version of our manuscript.
- Figure S3: FSC curves indicates the mask during refinement is too tight and could be optimized
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. However, the unique architecture of K2P channels
allows detergent micelles to occupy grooves formed between various secondary structure
elements in the transmembrane region. Moreover, the detergent that we used for purification is
DMNG. Neopentyl glycol class of detergents has low CMCs and are known to form
heterogeneous micelles with varying sizes depending on the effective concentration of the
detergent 27. To avoid heterogeneity in micelle size and stochastic detergent densities from
interfering with refinement, we had to use a relatively tight mask to reconstruct a map with
interpretable features at the protein-micelle interface. We have tried to dilate the mask more, and
the resulting structure could not reach as high a resolution as the current map. A relatively tight
mask is needed to effectively remove the micelle density that is tightly bound to our protein.
- Could the authors mention/indicate the possible glycosylation sites that TWIK-2 possesses?
This could be added to S1.
We have now highlighted the glycosylation sites N79 and N85 on the sequence alignment (current
Figure S2).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have now addressed all of my remaining concern and I recommend for publication
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
We thank and congratulate the authors for the thorough revision and the inclusion of a significant bulk of new data. The work as gained in substance, providing a solid contribution to the field and merits publication.
Minor comments to help the authors in the final revision of the manuscript (If taken care of, no need to be checked again by me).
1. The authors have now included the mutant Y111A alongside the originally used Y111H, which shows some differences in the activation and inhibition profile. However, the differences are not always clearly stated. One example can be found on page 12: "Moreover, we notice a reduction in maximum inhibition for NPBA in M135A, S213A, and the T106A-T214A double mutants of TWIK-2 (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5C)." However, according to the figures, Y111A/H should also be added in the sentence. In particular Fig S5 shows that Y111A goes from a significant 80% NPBA-inhibition to 40%. When Y111A is added to this statement the subsequent sentences will require revision too: "These mutants outline a pocket underneath the SF in the central vestibule (Fig. 3A). Based on these observations, we hypothesize that NPBA diffuses through the fenestration site and binds underneath the SF in the central vestibule.”
2. Adjust statement on top of page 5: "As we used HEK293 GnTI- cells, which lack N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase I activity, for the overexpression of TWIK-2, glycosylation at these sites is prevented. Glycosylation at these sites may be necessary for stabilization of this loop region". --> This is not entirely true. GntI- cells limit N-linked glycosylation of expressed glycoproteins to a pattern dominated by the Man GlcNAc N-glycan, and therefore result in a more "homogenous" glycosylation of the protein. Hence, better to rephrase that a more complex glycosylation than the shorter and more homogenous produced by GnTI- cells might be the cause.
3. End of page 7, top of page 8: "We compared the IC50 values of wild-type TWIK-2 against four mutants: one each at the entry (Y111) and exit (M135) of the ion permeation pore, as well as two at the bottom of selectivity filters SF1 (T106A) and SF2 (T214A)." --> Please indicate to which residues Y111 and M135 have been mutated into. It is indicated later in the text, so I suspect this is just an oversight.
4. Correct sentence on Page 8: "For ML365, the maximum inhibition remained similar to that of wild-type TWIK-2 in all variants, except for the T106A-T214A double mutant, which showed. In the case of ML365, we noticed that the maximum inhibition for all the variants remained similar to wild-type TWIK-2, except the T106A-T214A double mutant, where we saw a significant reduction"
5. Page 13: The original conclusion paragraph is missing. Ignore if this was intentional.
6. Methods section, data processing: Please indicate whether the last refinement was still done with C1symmetry.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank all the reviewers for their critical assessment of our manuscript. Our point-by-point response is below. For purposes of clarity, we have reviewer comments in red italics.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
“This study determines a TWIK2 cryoEM structure and uses a commercial automated patch clamp setup to assess the function of TWIK2 channel mutants and pharmacology. The structure of TWIK2 had not been previously determined and this study provides a first look at the TWIK2 channel architecture. To accompany the structure, the authors perform electrophysiological recordings of TWIK2, a channel that has been notoriously difficult (though not impossible) to record from. Overall, the methodology in the structural and functional work appears to be sound and the writing is clear. “
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the overall positive feedback.
“There are novel observations and interesting results in the manuscript but an informative connection between knowledge learned from the TWIK2 structure and the functional studies performed is largely lacking. The Y111H designed to mimic the TWIK1 pH sensing histidine and the S4 site threonine residues are all positions that did not require a cryoEM structure to be interesting candidates for mutation. While the M135A mutation is a candidate site based on the TWIK2 structure, it is unclear why the authors chose this position as it does not occlude the pore or play any clearly observable role in the TWIK2 structure. The experiments examining the effects of ML365 and NPBA are interesting but somewhat superficial, as the mutants show some effects on channel pharmacology but do not yield any substantive insight into where the drugs might bind or how they might act.”
We thank the reviewer for pointing out weaknesses in this manuscript that could be improved. We agree with the reviewer that the mutant selection was sparse. To address this, the analysis in the revised version of the manuscript includes the following single and double mutants: F98A, Y111H, Y111A, T106A, T214A, S213A, M135N, M135A, and T106A-T214A, focusing on the regions near the SF, the K2P modulator pocket (F98A), and the hydrophobic cuff (M135A and M135N). The alanine substitution of M135 (M135A) drastically reduces the size of the side chain, affecting not only the size of the pocket near M135 but also the relative hydrophobic surface area. As we observed lipid-like densities around the M135 amino acid, suggesting their role in regulating channel activity, we anticipated that the M135A mutation would have a drastic effect on TWIK-2 activity. In the revised manuscript, we also tested M135N to explore the role of introducing a polar amino acid in this region on TWIK-2 activity. We observe that both M135A and M135N mutants exhibit slightly slower channel activation, with no drastic effect on channel activity. However, M135A shows a greater loss of NPBA inhibition compared to M135N, suggesting that removing the bulky amino acid at this position affects the efficacy of NPBA. Similarly, we also tested the effect of changing the pocket around Y111 on TWIK-2 channel activity using a Y111A mutant. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition, highlighting the role of Y111 in maintaining SF1-M2 loop integrity.
To study the binding modes of ML365 and NPBA, we collected and analyzed cryo-EM data using TWIK-2 complexed with ML365 and NPBA. We observed that in the presence of these ligands, the sample appeared to be more heterogeneous, resulting in maps of lower quality compared to the apo TWIK-2 map reported in this manuscript. The resolutions of both the inhibitor-bound TWIK-2 maps are fairly similar (~ 4 Å), with one common feature being the loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities that we observed in apo-TWIK-2 near the hydrophobic cuff. Of course, it is possible that loss of tubular lipid-like densities is a factor of poor resolution of the map. To make reasonable comparisons, we filtered the apo-TWIK-2 map to 4Å (Response Fig. 1).
Response Figure 1: cryo-EM map comparison of TWIK-2 Apo, TWIK-2 ML365 and TWIK-2 NPBA. Two bottom views on the right indicate the occupancy of the cavity close to the selectivity filter (top) and cytoplasmic site (bottom).
While we do not see any additional non-protein density in the ML365 dataset, we do observe some non-protein density immediately below the SF in the case of the NPBA dataset. The non-protein density that we see in the NPBA dataset is not seen in the apo TWIK-2; however, the poor resolution of the map, and the size and shape of the density, preclude us from unambiguously modeling NPBA at this site. Hence, we have not included these efforts in the manuscript and are presenting them here in the rebuttal. As the efforts to obtain high-resolution inhibitor-bound structures were not successful, we employed site-directed mutagenesis to identify a potential NPBA binding site by performing more mutations in the SF, K2P modulator pocket, and around the hydrophobic cuff. We have discussed these in the main manuscript and our findings suggest that the potential binding site for NPBA, as hinted by additional density in the map, could be below the SF. The mutagenesis exploration still does not identify the site for ML365 unambiguously. However, loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities around the hydrophobic cuff compared to apo TWIK-2 makes us suspect that ML365, like NPBA could bind through the cavity, albeit interacting with different residues compared to NPBA.
“1) In the section entitled “Ion conduction pore of TWIK2”, the authors suggest that the carbonyl oxygens of selectivity filter residues V107 and Y109 face away from the central permeation axis in TWIK-2 and argue for the relevance of this SF orientation to TWIK2 function. Given the ~3.7 angstrom resolution of the overall structure, I cannot ascertain how the authors come to this conclusion. Using the map and model provided by the authors, I can easily model the selectivity filter within the map in a conventional orientation and find that I improve the number of residues in favored orientations when the SF is modeled more conventionally.
If there is a biophysical argument to be made that the positioning of the valine and tyrosine sidechains in the TWIK2 map somehow promote an unconventional SF backbone configuration, this should be provided. Simply based on the map provided by the authors, I find this section to be unsupported by experimental results. If the authors do feel their selectivity figure configuration is accurate, a supplemental figure showing how the experimental map is better fit by the outward rather than inward-facing carbonyls at V107 and Y109 would be extremely helpful to make the authors' case on this point.”
We thank the reviewer for a thorough review of our structure. In our TWIK-2 structure, the SF has been modeled with carbonyl oxygens of three amino acids – V107, Y109, and L217 – facing away from the ion-conductance pore. While we agree that at ~ 3.7 Å resolution it could be challenging to resolve the orientation of carbonyl oxygens in the dynamic loops of the SF region unambiguously, we would like to highlight that the local resolution for this region is much better than 3.5 Å (Supplementary Fig. S3F in the manuscript). As per the reviewer’s critique, we attempted to model these three carbonyls in various combinations of them facing away or towards the SF. However, just based on visually comparing the fits of these various models to density, it is not straight forward to identity one particular combination of the carbonyl oxygens that fits better to the map (see figures & table below). Hence, based on a comparison of the model statistics such as bond RMSDs, Ramachandran outliers, Rama-Z score, & CaBLAM outliers for the SF region, and the overall model quality statistics for the whole protein, we believe that the model as it has been presented in the manuscript is the best possible fit (Response Table 1 in this rebuttal).
In K2P channels, the two conserved threonines at the bottom of the selectivity filter (SF) are the only amino acids within the SF that coordinate K+ ions through their side chains. All other amino acids at the SF coordinate K+ ions through carbonyl oxygens. It has been shown by multiple groups previously that reorientation of the carbonyl oxygens away from the SF is a means to regulate K+ ion flow, including channel inhibition, in potassium channels. Using X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, several groups have shown that reorientation of carbonyl oxygens away from the SF pore affects the K+ ion coordination at the SF as part of C-type or pH-mediated inactivation of the channel in KcsA, Kv, and TWIK-11–4. The flipped carbonyls often co-existed with reduced occupancy at the canonical K+ ion sites (S0-S4) in the SF. As noted in the manuscript, our cryo-EM map allowed us to confidently model K+ ions in only three out of these five sites. Similarly, MD simulations on the prototypical K+ channels like MthK and KcsA have shown that reorientation of the carbonyl oxygen of the conserved valine at the SF is one of the initial steps that promotes dissociation of K+ from the SF and allows the SF to adopt nonconducting or inactivated states5,6. As pointed out by the reviewer, we had provided only a brief biophysical explanation for non-canonical carbonyl positioning in the discussion in the original manuscript. To address that, we have expanded on the explanation associated with flipped carbonyl observation, by including examples of other eukaryotic K+ channels (TWIK-1, Kv, and Kir) and their prototypic prokaryotic homologs (MthK and KcsA) where similar observations have been made, as a separate section in the discussion, & added more references to this section.
Response Figure 2: Various TWIK2 selectivity filter models fit to the cryo-EM density. The model quality statistics for the variations 1-7, and a comparison of the statistics are provided in table 1. Cryo-EM density is highlighted as blue mesh and the three K+ ions as blue spheres. The two protomers, TWIK-2 chain A and B, are colored light magenta and light cyan. All the amino acids at the SF are labeled in variation 7 where none of the carbonyls are flipped away from the SF, and in the remaining panels only the carbonyls that are flipped away from the SF have been labeled.
