## Methods

Cloning and overexpression of recombinant TWIK-2
The codon-optimized full-length wild-type human TWIK-2 (KCNK6) was synthesized by GenScript and was subcloned into the pEGBacMam expression vector (Addgene plasmid #160683) to be expressed with an N-terminal Strep-tag-II, followed by a GFP tag and an HRV-3C protease site. TWIK-2 mutations (F98A, T106A, Y111A, Y111H, M135A, M135N, S213A, T214A, T106A/T214A) were also made in this background by GenScript. Wild-type (TWIK-2) and variants of TWIK-2 were expressed in HEK293 GnTI− cells (ATCC #CRL-3022). Large-scale protein production was done using a baculoviral expression system as per the protocol described by Goehring et al.74. Briefly, the TWIK-2 expression vector was transformed into chemically competent DH10Bac cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and white colonies were selected on gentamicin-kanamycin-tetracycline LB agar plates. Isolated Bacmid DNA was used to transfect sf9 cells (ATCC #12659017) with Cellfectin-II reagent (Gibco) per the manufacturer’s protocol to make baculovirus P1. P1 was then amplified to make P2 by adding 200 μl of P1 to 200 ml culture of sf9 cells at a 1×106 cells/ml density. Cells were grown at 27°C for 96 h and harvested by spinning at 4000×g for 20 min. The supernatant was filtered with a 0.22 μm filter and stored at 4°C in the dark as a P2 virus. This was subsequently used for large-scale transduction of HEK293 GnTI− suspension adapted cells grown in FreeStyle 293 media supplemented with 2% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) at density of 2.5–3.0×106 cells/ml. Transduced cells were incubated on an orbital shaker at 37°C and 8% CO2 at 120 rpm. Eight hours after transduction, 10 mM Sodium butyrate was added, and cells were grown for an additional 16–24 h at 37°C, 8% CO2. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4000×g for 20 min, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C.

Purification of recombinant human TWIK-2
Cell pellets from 2.4 L culture were thawed and lysed in 120 ml lysis buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.8 μM aprotinin, 2 μg/ml leupeptin, 2 μM pepstatin A, 1 mM PMSF, pH 7.5) by sonication. Lysed cells were centrifuged at 2400×g for 5 min to remove cell debris. The supernatant was then ultracentrifuged at 185,000×g for 45 min. The pellet from ultracentrifugation was resuspended using a Dounce homogenizer in 60 ml of lysis buffer. To solubilize the membrane, 60 ml 2X solubilization buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.8 μM aprotinin, 2 μg/ml leupeptin, 2 μM pepstatin A, 1 mM PMSF, 2% DMNG, pH 7.5) was added, and the solubilization was carried out for 90 min at 4°C. The solubilized membrane was then centrifuged at 185,000×g for 1 h. The supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter and was loaded onto a column containing 3 ml Strep-Tactin resin (IBA Life Sciences) at a flow rate of 0.5 ml/min. The column was then washed with 15 ml of wash buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.1% DMNG, pH 7.5) and eluted with 12 ml elution buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, 0.1% DMNG, 5 mM Desthiobiotin, pH 7.5) in 1.5 ml fractions. The homogeneity of eluted fractions was analyzed by SDS-PAGE and subsequently pooled and concentrated to 7 mg/ml. In-house purified HRV3C protease was added to purified TWIK-2 at a molar ratio of 1:20 and incubated overnight at 4°C to remove the GFP tag. The digested protein was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) pre-equilibrated with SEC buffer (0.1% DMNG, 25 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM KCl, pH 7.5). The fractions corresponding to GFP-tag-free TWIK-2 dimer were pooled and concentrated to 2.3 mg/ml for cryo-EM sample preparation.

Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection
UltraAuFoil 300 mesh 1.2/1.3 grids (Quantifoil) were glow discharged (PELCO) for 60 s at 15 mA before use. 3.5 μl purified TWIK-2 was applied to the glow-discharged grids and blotted for 2.5–3 s at 4°C and 100% humidity using a Vitrobot (Mark IV, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Grids were immediately plunged-frozen in liquid ethane. Grids were screened, and movies were collected at the University of Michigan cryo-EM facility on 300 kV Titan Krios G4i cryo-EM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with K3 direct detector camera (Gatan), and a post-BioQuantum GIF energy filter (Gatan), slit width set to 20 eV. 15,006 movies were collected using SerialEM 4.0 software in counting mode at a magnification of 105,000× (nominal pixel size of 0.83 Å/pixel). The total dose was 60 e− Å−2 with 60 frames with a defocus range between 0.8 and 2.5 μm.

Cryo-EM data processing
Data processing was performed in cryoSPARC (version 4.5.3)75 Briefly, 15,006 movie stacks were motion corrected and patch-CTF estimated, followed by a manual curation to remove micrographs with relatively thick ice and CTF fit >7 Å. 10,629 micrographs were subsequently selected and used for reference-free particle picking by blob picker with minimum particle diameter of 80 Å and maximum particle diameter of 100 Å followed by extraction at a box size of 256 pixels at binning of 2. 5,447,554 particles were picked and subjected to two rounds of 2D classification that resulted in 1,387,475 relative particles. A subset of ~380,000 particles from 2D classes with clear secondary structure features were used to generate four ab-initio 3D classes with C1 symmetry. One “good” class with clear transmembrane features and one “bad” class representing empty micelle were selected as reference input for downstream heterogeneous refinement with the total relatively clean 1,387,475 particles. Multiple rounds of heterogeneous refinement were performed until no further improvement of the resolution. 301,000 selected particles from the best class after the last heterogeneous refinement were re-extracted with 256 pixels and subjected to one round of Non-uniform refinement with C1 symmetry. A 3D mask was generated using volume of the best ab-initio class in Chimera 1.17.1 by manually removing the micelle density and imported into cryoSPARC with a threshold of 0.064 and dilation radius of 3 pixels. This mask was used for a focused 3D classification of the clean re-extracted particles into 4 classes in cryoSPARC. 104,997 particles from the class with clear secondary structure features were selected for reference-based motion correction, and refined by non-uniform refinement with C1 symmetry to obtain a final map at ~3.7 Å.

Model building, refinement, and structure analysis
The sharpened map from the final non-uniform refinement in cryoSPARC was used to build a preliminary model in Model Angelo 1.076. The preliminary model was analyzed, and improperly built regions were rebuilt manually in Coot 0.9.8.8377. Final structure refinement was performed in Phenix 1.2178. Figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX 1.1779. The radii along the channel pore were calculated using HOLE80. FoldX was used to generate mutant models of TWIK-281.

Automated patch clamp recordings
The wild-type and mutant TWIK-2 expression constructs were used to transfect adherent HEK293 GnTI− cells for automated whole-cell patch-clamp recordings. In brief, 1–7 million cells, grown in DMEM medium with 10% FBS, were transfected at a density of approximately 0.6–0.7 million cells/mL using 1–4 µg of DNA and TurboFect, following the manufacturer’s instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After an 8-h incubation, the media was replaced with fresh DMEM containing 10 mM sodium butyrate, and the cells incubated for another 16–24 h before use. The cells were maintained at 37°C, 8% CO2, and 100% humidity. Before experiments, the cells were centrifuged at 200×g for 5 min, and the resulting pellet was resuspended in an external recording solution (see below) to achieve a final density of 500,000 cells/mL. This cell suspension was transferred to the instrument cell hotel, kept at 10°C, and shaken at 200 rpm until recordings began.

Automated patch clamp recordings were carried out using the Syncropatch 384 PE platform (Nanion Technologies, Munich, Germany). We used four-hole, 384-well recording chips with medium resistance between 2 and 4 MΩ. Pulse generation and data collection were managed with the PatchController384 V.1.3.0 and DataController384 V1.2.1 software (Nanion Technologies). Whole-cell currents were filtered at 3 kHz and sampled at 10 kHz. Access resistance and apparent membrane capacitance were estimated using the built-in protocols. Recordings were obtained from cells expressing both wild-type and mutant K2P channels at room temperature, with an internal solution containing 110 mM KF, 10 mM KCl, 10 mM NaCl, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM EGTA, with pH adjusted to 7.2 using KOH. The external solution included 44 mM NaCl, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2, and 5 mM glucose, buffered with 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.4, adjusted with NaOH) or 10 mM MES (pH 5.5, adjusted with NaOH). Recordings were only accepted from cells that showed a seal resistance greater than 100 MΩ, a series resistance below 10 MΩ, and stable cell capacitance throughout the session. To assess the biophysical properties of wild-type and mutant TWIK channels, we measured both current density and potassium ion reversal potential (Vrev). Whole-cell currents were recorded from a holding potential of −90 mV and elicited with depolarizing steps (200 ms) from −90 to +100 mV in 10 mV increments, followed by a return step to −90 mV (tail currents, 100 ms), and current–voltage (I–V) relationships were plotted for each condition. The voltage reversal potential (Vrev) was identified from the I–V curve as the membrane potential where no net current was observed. Current density was calculated by normalizing the peak current amplitude at the highest voltage step to the cell’s membrane capacitance, which accounts for differences in cell size. Tail currents measured 1 ms after returning to −90 mV were normalized to their maximum amplitude and graphed against the test potential (−90 to +100 mV). To find the voltage at half-maximal activation (V50) and the slope factor (k), normalized G–V curves were fitted with the Boltzmann equation:

G=1=(1+exp[(V-V50)=k]) (1)

The properties of each TWIK-2 mutant were compared to those of the wild-type (WT) channel measured in parallel, focusing on the difference (ΔV50) in voltage-dependent activation V50.

To evaluate the effect of small molecules on TWIK-2 channel activity, the test compound was applied to the extracellular face (cap domain) of the channel using an external solution. A depolarization step to +60 mV was then performed for 350 ms, starting from a holding potential of -90 mV, and this procedure was repeated every 5 s. During each depolarization, the peak outward current amplitude was carefully measured and normalized to the currents recorded before the addition of the compounds. For the concentration-response curves (CRCs), various concentrations of the compounds were applied across the four-hole, 384-well recording chip, or a single high concentration of 50 µM was used to achieve maximum blocking. Electrophysiological responses were analyzed in detail by calculating the ratios of peak currents in the presence (Icompound) and absence (I0) of the test compounds. Data analysis and graphing were performed using DataController384 V.3.2.0 (Nanion Technologies) and GraphPad Prism V.10.5.0, with concentration-response curves fitted to a three-parameter sigmoidal model. The rates of channel activation and deactivation were determined by fitting the outward currents elicited at +60 mV and the tail currents during -90 mV pulses to a single exponential function using DataController384 from Nanion Technologies. The number of cells used for each experimental condition is listed in the figure legends. Detailed statistical methods were also described in the figure legends.

Drug and reagents
K2P modulator ML365 (Sigma-Aldrich SML2643), NPBA (MedChemExpress), ML335 (MedChemExpress), and BL1249 (Tocris) were diluted to 20 mM in sterile DMSO (Sigma-Aldrich) and stored in -80°C before use.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This study determines a TWIK2 cryoEM structure and uses a commercial automated patch clamp setup to assess the function of TWIK2 channel mutants and pharmacology. The structure of TWIK2 had not been previously determined and this study provides a first look at the TWIK2 channel architecture. To accompany the structure, the authors perform electrophysiological recordings of TWIK2, a channel that has been notoriously difficult (though not impossible) to record from. Overall, the methodology in the structural and functional work appears to be sound and the writing is clear. There are novel observations and interesting results in the manuscript but an informative connection between knowledge learned from the TWIK2 structure and the functional studies performed is largely lacking. The Y111H designed to mimic the TWIK1 pH sensing histidine and the S4 site threonine residues are all positions that did not require a cryoEM structure to be interesting candidates for mutation. While the M135A mutation is a candidate site based on the TWIK2 structure, it is unclear why the authors chose this position as it does not occlude the pore or play any clearly observable role in the TWIK2 structure. The experiments examining the effects of ML365 and NPBA are interesting but somewhat superficial, as the mutants show some effects on channel pharmacology but do not yield any substantive insight into where the drugs might bind or how they might act.

Major Points
1) In the section entitled “Ion conduction pore of TWIK2”, the authors suggest that the carbonyl oxygens of selectivity filter residues V107 and Y109 face away from the central permeation axis in TWIK-2 and argue for the relevance of this SF orientation to TWIK2 function. Given the ~3.7 angstrom resolution of the overall structure, I cannot ascertain how the authors come to this conclusion. Using the map and model provided by the authors, I can easily model the selectivity filter within the map in a conventional orientation and find that I improve the number of residues in favored orientations when the SF is modeled more conventionally.
If there is a biophysical argument to be made that the positioning of the valine and tyrosine sidechains in the TWIK2 map somehow promote an unconventional SF backbone configuration, this should be provided. Simply based on the map provided by the authors, I find this section to be unsupported by experimental results. If the authors do feel their selectivity figure configuration is accurate, a supplemental figure showing how the experimental map is better fit by the outward rather than inward facing carbonyls at V107 and Y109 would be extremely helpful to make the authors case on this point.
2) In Figure 2B, the pore radius profile shows a constriction of the pore at around 5A from the cytoplasmic face of the channel. This cytoplasmic constriction does not seem to be discussed in the manuscript. Is this constriction brought about by the lipids modeled in the structure? If so, is this at all relevant to the function of TWIK2? If the authors believe that these lipid densities are important to shaping the TWIK2 pore, then this pore radius plot is appropriate. If the relevance of these lipids is unclear and could simply be an artifact of the protein purification process, it would be better to omit the lipid densities when running HOLE (or include a second HOLE profile in the absence of the lipids) to show the profile of just the TWIK2 protein. It would also be appropriate to discuss the lipid densities present in the map in the results section of the manuscript, rather than the discussion. This would be a good spot to do so.
3) For the experiments where G/GMAX–V curves are calculated, it does not appear that the recordings reach a steady state at 200 ms. The current is still rising for TWIK1 wt and this is even more pronounced in the mutants that slow activation (Figure 3B). Is it possible that the differences in V50 are artifactual, since the maximal steady state current is reached at 200ms in some of the mutants but not in all of them.
4) I think the manuscript would be greatly improved by a more direct comparison of the TWIK2 structure with the previously published TWIK1 structures. Does this TWIK2 structure look more like the low pH or neutral pH TWIK2 structure? Are there clear differences in the positioning of the cap or TM helices? The entire section of the results devoted to an overview of the TWIK2 channel could be redone as a more direct comparison between TWIK1 and TWIK2 and would significantly increase interest.

Minor Points
- In the introduction, “Kcnk6 knockout studies have shown suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages, implicating endolysosomal localization of TWIK-2 in inflammation 45,46.” This sentence is a bit misleading and should be clarified. From the references cited, it is movement of TWIK2 from the endolysosome to the plasma membrane that appears to be a critical step in the potassium efflux that mediates NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
- In figure 1 (and for nearly all electrophysiological traces shown in the manuscript), recording traces are shown on a signal scale that reads “Normalized I”. It is unclear what the non-transfected cells traces are normalized to? For clarity throughout the manuscript, it would be helpful if the authors explicitly discuss whether normalization was applied using a universal metric (which could be described in the methods section of the manuscript) or ad hoc for each set of recordings (in which case this should be described in each figure legends)
- Given that the C-terminally truncated TWIK construct was not used for structure of detailed functional studies, this data could be omitted or moved to the methods section.
- Is it meaningful that the loop region between V75-P89 is unresolved in the cryo-EM structure? In all other K2P structures, this loop is well resolved. Does this mean that the V75-P89 is dynamic in TWIK2, suggestive of a functional role? Or is this just a limitation of the resolutions of this TWIK2 structure compared to other K2P structures? Does 3D variability analysis in cryosparc give any indication of what is going on in this loop region?
- The panel in Figure 3 showing the relative locations of T106, T214, M135, and Y111 is critically important for understanding the orientation and relevance of these residues. I would suggest reworking this figure to make it clearer. The inset boxes are distracting, as each one has a different orientation relative to the main panel. Perhaps a clearly labeled “top view” showing the Y111 residues, “bottom view showing the M135 residues, and a side view like shown in the left side of Figure 3A would be sufficient for this.
- “Notably, TWIK-2 channels elicited outward potassium currents that increased with depolarization (over +30 mV), suggesting voltage-dependent activation of TWIK-2” Isn’t this a surprising result, given that prior recordings in symmetrical potassium have shown inward rectification rather than outward rectification? Is there any methodologic explanation for this difference in observed functional behavior?
- Reference 70 in the manuscript includes data that describe the effect of mutations at the S4 site threonines in K2Ps. For nearly all K2Ps, these S4 site mutations cause a loss of volage dependance. It is therefore interesting that in TWIK2, the T106A and T214A mutants maintain their voltage dependent gating. Is there any rationale for why this might be the case?
- “Mutations T106A and T214A disturb these networks of hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions that stabilize the base of the SF and make the channel less selective and more open (Figure 3B-3F).” The functional experiments presented in this section use only a single ionic composition and are not suited to adequately address ion selectivity. Please support with data or omit this claim.
- Is the TWIK2 Y111H mutant pH sensitive like the TWIK1 channel? This seems like an obvious experiment to try and would be informative to understanding differences between TWIK1 and TWIK2 function.
- More methodological detail of the automated patch clamp technique would be helpful to understand the experimental system. Are drugs applied to the intracellular face of the channel (via syncropatch pipette) or extracellular via bath?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript of Ma et al, provides new insights into the modulation of the K2P channel TWIK-2 using structural and electrophysiological data. The study provides the first cryo-EM structure of the full-length TWIK-2 at 3.7Å resolution, which is accompanied by mutagenesis studies and the use of a whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology workflow. The authors show that TWIK-2 is pH-insensitive but slightly voltage-gated, and suggest potential different binding modes or mechanisms of inhibition in TWIK-2 for two of the four tested K2P modulators (ML365 and NPBA).
The work is well executed and well written. However, overall the study fall a bit short. The new insights provided do not represent a big step forward in improving our understanding of how TWIK-2 (and K2P channels in general) function and are regulated. The substance and depth of the study could be/have been strengthened by more structure-guided mutagenesis studies, a more robust comparison of their new automated electrophysiology setup, a better literature comparison with (mutagenesis studies of) TWIK-1 and other K2P channels, or even more structural data or structural analysis. While I understand that addressing them all might be out of the scope of this study, the manuscript requires a bit more of depth.
Specific suggestion would be (major comments):
1. In total ‘only’ four residues are identified as different/interesting and tested. Namely M135A, T106A, T214A and Y111H. What about other positions, e.g., around the cavity or along the ion conductance pathway? Is everything else conserved? What about testing mutating the same sites with other substitutes or using double and triple mutations to gain more insights? Compare in more depth with TWIK-1 and other K2P channels.
2. Most striking in this endeavor is the mutant Y111H. The authors show that in contrast to TWIK-1, TWIK-2 is pH-insensitive, with the histidine in that position being the pH-sensing residue in TWIK-1. While the authors go on and attempt to describe some of the differences observed for TWIK-2-Y111H, they never actually tested if this mutant has become pH-sensitive. Considering the overall conservation between TWIK-1 and TWIK-2 this would be expected and highly interesting to test. Further, to test the importance of the tyrosine and decouple it from a pH sensor position, a mutation to another residue, e.g. Y111A and Y111L would be interesting. Finally, the fact that TWIK-2_Y111H mutant carries the pH sensor of TWIK-1 must be mentioned in all clarity also in the results and discussion section and taking into account during interpretation.
3. I appreciate and highly welcome the high-throughput patch clamp workflow presented by the authors. However, considering i) the discrepancies mentioned by the authors on electrophysiology studies for TWIK-2 in the literature, and ii) the mentioned inconsistencies between some of their electrophysiology data with that published before, the authors should do a more thorough comparison. If possible, between methods conducted by themselves with the same non-glycosylated constructs (conventional patch clamp and high-throughput patch clamp). But perhaps more importantly, use TWIK-1 in their automated whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology setup, for which more robust recordings have been reported. This would allow to asses and compare TWIK-1 and TWIK-2 and the different workflows better.
4. The slightly different impact found for two of the tested inhibitors makes the discussion a bit ambiguous as to their potential different binding mode. I wonder if an attempt to solve an inhibitor-bound structure would be in the scope of this study as the authors seem to be able to obtain enough stable protein and the processing appears rather straightforward.
Other major comments:
5. Can the authors comment on the following: With regards to the processing of the cryo-EM data, I wonder if the authors also tested refining the other 3 classes obtained before proceeding with a final NU-refinement of one of the classes. Considering the authors interpret their structure as an intermediate conductive state, I wonder if there were some hints at other conformational states captured in the data.
6. Could the authors comment why they mutated Y111H to mimic the corresponding TWIK-1 residue, but then mutated M135A instead of M135L (which would be the corresponding TWIK-1 residue)? What was the rational/strategy here? And here again, it would have been ideal to have TWIK-1 as a control experiment, and to compare Y111H with.
7. Could the authors comment/expand on the voltage-dependence of TWIK-2 in the, and whether other K2P channels have also been found to be so.
8. While I appreciate the modeling of potential lipids and co for the interpretation and figure rendering of non-protein densities, considering the high ambiguity, I expect that the authors have no intention of including it in the to be deposited model. (in the era of AlphaFold and machine learning, everything that is deposited can and will be use by AI or others)
Minor comments:
- Page 4: "we identified key amino acids that differentiate TWIK-2 from TWIK-1 and other members of the K2P family". From what I understood, only Y111 was a direct comparison with TWIK-1, so I suggest toning down this sentence.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We thank all the reviewers for their critical assessment of our manuscript. Our point-by-point response is below. For purposes of clarity, we have reviewer comments in red italics.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
“This study determines a TWIK2 cryoEM structure and uses a commercial automated patch clamp setup to assess the function of TWIK2 channel mutants and pharmacology. The structure of TWIK2 had not been previously determined and this study provides a first look at the TWIK2 channel architecture. To accompany the structure, the authors perform electrophysiological recordings of TWIK2, a channel that has been notoriously difficult (though not impossible) to record from. Overall, the methodology in the structural and functional work appears to be sound and the writing is clear. “
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the overall positive feedback.
“There are novel observations and interesting results in the manuscript but an informative connection between knowledge learned from the TWIK2 structure and the functional studies performed is largely lacking. The Y111H designed to mimic the TWIK1 pH sensing histidine and the S4 site threonine residues are all positions that did not require a cryoEM structure to be interesting candidates for mutation. While the M135A mutation is a candidate site based on the TWIK2 structure, it is unclear why the authors chose this position as it does not occlude the pore or play any clearly observable role in the TWIK2 structure. The experiments examining the effects of ML365 and NPBA are interesting but somewhat superficial, as the mutants show some effects on channel pharmacology but do not yield any substantive insight into where the drugs might bind or how they might act.”
We thank the reviewer for pointing out weaknesses in this manuscript that could be improved. We agree with the reviewer that the mutant selection was sparse. To address this, the analysis in the revised version of the manuscript includes the following single and double mutants: F98A, Y111H, Y111A, T106A, T214A, S213A, M135N, M135A, and T106A-T214A, focusing on the regions near the SF, the K2P modulator pocket (F98A), and the hydrophobic cuff (M135A and M135N). The alanine substitution of M135 (M135A) drastically reduces the size of the side chain, affecting not only the size of the pocket near M135 but also the relative hydrophobic surface area. As we observed lipid-like densities around the M135 amino acid, suggesting their role in regulating channel activity, we anticipated that the M135A mutation would have a drastic effect on TWIK-2 activity. In the revised manuscript, we also tested M135N to explore the role of introducing a polar amino acid in this region on TWIK-2 activity. We observe that both M135A and M135N mutants exhibit slightly slower channel activation, with no drastic effect on channel activity. However, M135A shows a greater loss of NPBA inhibition compared to M135N, suggesting that removing the bulky amino acid at this position affects the efficacy of NPBA. Similarly, we also tested the effect of changing the pocket around Y111 on TWIK-2 channel activity using a Y111A mutant. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition, highlighting the role of Y111 in maintaining SF1-M2 loop integrity.
To study the binding modes of ML365 and NPBA, we collected and analyzed cryo-EM data using TWIK-2 complexed with ML365 and NPBA. We observed that in the presence of these ligands, the sample appeared to be more heterogeneous, resulting in maps of lower quality compared to the apo TWIK-2 map reported in this manuscript. The resolutions of both the inhibitor-bound TWIK-2 maps are fairly similar (~ 4 Å), with one common feature being the loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities that we observed in apo-TWIK-2 near the hydrophobic cuff. Of course, it is possible that loss of tubular lipid-like densities is a factor of poor resolution of the map. To make reasonable comparisons, we filtered the apo-TWIK-2 map to 4Å (Response Fig. 1).
Response Figure 1: cryo-EM map comparison of TWIK-2 Apo, TWIK-2 ML365 and TWIK-2 NPBA. Two bottom views on the right indicate the occupancy of the cavity close to the selectivity filter (top) and cytoplasmic site (bottom).
While we do not see any additional non-protein density in the ML365 dataset, we do observe some non-protein density immediately below the SF in the case of the NPBA dataset. The non-protein density that we see in the NPBA dataset is not seen in the apo TWIK-2; however, the poor resolution of the map, and the size and shape of the density, preclude us from unambiguously modeling NPBA at this site. Hence, we have not included these efforts in the manuscript and are presenting them here in the rebuttal. As the efforts to obtain high-resolution inhibitor-bound structures were not successful, we employed site-directed mutagenesis to identify a potential NPBA binding site by performing more mutations in the SF, K2P modulator pocket, and around the hydrophobic cuff. We have discussed these in the main manuscript and our findings suggest that the potential binding site for NPBA, as hinted by additional density in the map, could be below the SF. The mutagenesis exploration still does not identify the site for ML365 unambiguously. However, loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities around the hydrophobic cuff compared to apo TWIK-2 makes us suspect that ML365, like NPBA could bind through the cavity, albeit interacting with different residues compared to NPBA.
“1) In the section entitled “Ion conduction pore of TWIK2”, the authors suggest that the carbonyl oxygens of selectivity filter residues V107 and Y109 face away from the central permeation axis in TWIK-2 and argue for the relevance of this SF orientation to TWIK2 function. Given the ~3.7 angstrom resolution of the overall structure, I cannot ascertain how the authors come to this conclusion. Using the map and model provided by the authors, I can easily model the selectivity filter within the map in a conventional orientation and find that I improve the number of residues in favored orientations when the SF is modeled more conventionally.
If there is a biophysical argument to be made that the positioning of the valine and tyrosine sidechains in the TWIK2 map somehow promote an unconventional SF backbone configuration, this should be provided. Simply based on the map provided by the authors, I find this section to be unsupported by experimental results. If the authors do feel their selectivity figure configuration is accurate, a supplemental figure showing how the experimental map is better fit by the outward rather than inward-facing carbonyls at V107 and Y109 would be extremely helpful to make the authors' case on this point.”
We thank the reviewer for a thorough review of our structure. In our TWIK-2 structure, the SF has been modeled with carbonyl oxygens of three amino acids – V107, Y109, and L217 – facing away from the ion-conductance pore. While we agree that at ~ 3.7 Å resolution it could be challenging to resolve the orientation of carbonyl oxygens in the dynamic loops of the SF region unambiguously, we would like to highlight that the local resolution for this region is much better than 3.5 Å (Supplementary Fig. S3F in the manuscript). As per the reviewer’s critique, we attempted to model these three carbonyls in various combinations of them facing away or towards the SF. However, just based on visually comparing the fits of these various models to density, it is not straight forward to identity one particular combination of the carbonyl oxygens that fits better to the map (see figures & table below). Hence, based on a comparison of the model statistics such as bond RMSDs, Ramachandran outliers, Rama-Z score, & CaBLAM outliers for the SF region, and the overall model quality statistics for the whole protein, we believe that the model as it has been presented in the manuscript is the best possible fit (Response Table 1 in this rebuttal).
In K2P channels, the two conserved threonines at the bottom of the selectivity filter (SF) are the only amino acids within the SF that coordinate K+ ions through their side chains. All other amino acids at the SF coordinate K+ ions through carbonyl oxygens. It has been shown by multiple groups previously that reorientation of the carbonyl oxygens away from the SF is a means to regulate K+ ion flow, including channel inhibition, in potassium channels. Using X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, several groups have shown that reorientation of carbonyl oxygens away from the SF pore affects the K+ ion coordination at the SF as part of C-type or pH-mediated inactivation of the channel in KcsA, Kv, and TWIK-11–4. The flipped carbonyls often co-existed with reduced occupancy at the canonical K+ ion sites (S0-S4) in the SF. As noted in the manuscript, our cryo-EM map allowed us to confidently model K+ ions in only three out of these five sites. Similarly, MD simulations on the prototypical K+ channels like MthK and KcsA have shown that reorientation of the carbonyl oxygen of the conserved valine at the SF is one of the initial steps that promotes dissociation of K+ from the SF and allows the SF to adopt nonconducting or inactivated states5,6. As pointed out by the reviewer, we had provided only a brief biophysical explanation for non-canonical carbonyl positioning in the discussion in the original manuscript. To address that, we have expanded on the explanation associated with flipped carbonyl observation, by including examples of other eukaryotic K+ channels (TWIK-1, Kv, and Kir) and their prototypic prokaryotic homologs (MthK and KcsA) where similar observations have been made, as a separate section in the discussion, & added more references to this section.

“2) In Figure 2B, the pore radius profile shows a constriction of the pore at around 5A from the cytoplasmic face of the channel. This cytoplasmic constriction does not seem to be discussed in the manuscript. Is this constriction brought about by the lipids modeled in the structure? If so, is this at all relevant to the function of TWIK2? If the authors believe that these lipid densities are important to shaping the TWIK2 pore, then this pore radius plot is appropriate. If the relevance of these lipids is unclear and could simply be an artifact of the protein purification process, it would be better to omit the lipid densities when running HOLE (or include a second HOLE profile in the absence of the lipids) to show the profile of just the TWIK2 protein.
It would also be appropriate to discuss the lipid densities present in the map in the results section of the manuscript, rather than the discussion. This would be a good spot to do so.”
The pore radius plot in Fig. 2B was constructed using the TWIK-2 model with hydrocarbon tails modeled into the tubular lipid-like densities. We have now edited Fig. 2B to show the pore radius profile with and without the modeled lipid-like densities. We did not include any exogenous lipids during the purification. So, we believe these tubular densities arise from the molecules that co-purified with TWIK-2 from HEK293 GnTI- cells. Because we could not verify the exact nature of these molecules, we have only modeled hydrocarbon tails in these densities and called them lipid-like in the manuscript. The discussion on the lipid-like densities has now been moved to the results section in the revised version of the manuscript, as per the reviewer’s suggestion. While this manuscript was under revision, another group reported a preprint suggesting a potential lipid mediated regulation of TWIK-2 channel activity. They argued that lipid molecules “plug” the channel on the cytoplasmic side by occupying the central cavity and by physically obstructing the passage of ions, rendering TWIK-2 inactive. They demonstrate that R257, an amino acid towards the C-terminus that lies below the hydrophobic cuff, is crucial for this lipid binding in the central cavity and that the R257A mutation increases the channel activity, suggesting that channel activation is a result of lipid removal or repositioning in the central cavity. In our TWIK-2 structure, we observe lipid-like densities in similar positions (central cavity and along the groove formed by the PH2, M2, and M4 helices) as reported by Mondal et al7. However, these lipid-like densities do not entirely obstruct the access to the central pore (Fig. 2). The observation of lipid-like density, corroborated by a different group independently, suggests that these molecules are relevant to the function. We have added a few lines discussing this preprint and its relevance in the context of our structure to the discussion section of the revised manuscript.
“3) For the experiments where G/GMAX–V curves are calculated, it does not appear that the recordings reach a steady state at 200 ms. The current is still rising for TWIK1 wt and this is even more pronounced in the mutants that slow activation (Figure 3B). Is it possible that the differences in V50 are artificial, since the maximal steady state current is reached at 200ms in some of the mutants but not in all of them.”
We appreciate the reviewer’s concerns regarding the possible underestimation of steady-state currents due to incomplete activation at the end of the 200-ms depolarizing pulse, especially in slow-activating TWIK-2 mutants. To reinforce the validity of our conclusions regarding mutant-induced shifts in voltage dependence, we performed a new analysis based on normalized tail currents, which better reflect the relative conductance by capturing the instantaneous current upon repolarization—thus minimizing the effects of kinetic differences in channel activation. Specifically, we constructed revised G/GMAX–V curves using tail currents, enabling a more accurate assessment of the voltage dependence of activation across all variants. From these curves, we calculated the ΔV50 values, which provide a more reliable measure of the voltage shift caused by each mutation. Importantly, this alternative approach produced similar V50 shifts as previously reported, confirming that the observed differences are genuine and not artifacts, reflecting fundamental changes in channel gating properties. These new results are now included in the revised Supplementary Fig. 5 and discussed in the Results section. To enable a better comparison of currents across TWIK-2 variants, we have also modified Fig. 3 to now display whole-cell current traces and activation time constants for all the mutants that we tested.
“4) I think the manuscript would be greatly improved by a more direct comparison of the TWIK2 structure with the previously published TWIK1 structures. Does this TWIK2 structure look more like the low pH or neutral pH TWIK2 structure? Are there clear differences in the positioning of the cap or TM helices? The entire section of the results devoted to an overview of the TWIK2 channel could be redone as a more direct comparison between TWIK1 and TWIK2 and would significantly increase interest.”
We agree with the reviewer that a comprehensive comparison of TWIK-2 with TWIK-1 could be a beneficial addition to the manuscript. In our first version of the manuscript, we had presented a comparison of TWIK-2 and TWIK-1 in Figs. 5B, C and Supplementary Fig. S4, focusing only on the conformational changes in pore domains, SF, and M4 helix. As TWIK-2 is physiologically unlike TWIK-1, for the sake of completeness, we have also included comparisons with other pH-sensitive and lipid-regulated K2P channels. To make these comparisons more apparent, we have reformatted and expanded the figures and text to include a separate comparison section of the TWIK-2 and TWIK-1 structures in their entirety. In addition, we have also included the results from whole-cell recordings studying the pH dependency of channel activity in TWIK-1 and the TWIK-1-like Y111H mutant of TWIK-2. Interestingly, we find that the differences in the structure of TWIK-2 are localized to the cap region when compared with the TWIK-1 structure at pH 7.5. When compared with TWIK-1 at pH 5.5, the differences lie only in the SF region, specifically the SF1-M2 linker that houses the pH-sensing amino acid H122 in TWIK-1. TWIK-2 has the cap region that is similar to inactive TWIK-1, but has the SF loops positioned in a similar way as that of the active TWIK-1, despite the residue Y111 in TWIK-2 (H122 in TWIK-1) adopting a unique ‘up’ conformation. These new observations have been discussed in the revised version of the manuscript, alongside the TWIK-2 and TWIK-1 comparisons from the older version (Fig. 1, 5). The comparison of TWIK-2 with other K2P channels has been reformatted into a separate figure (Supplementary Figs. 4, 7).
Minor Points
1. - In the introduction, “Kcnk6 knockout studies have shown suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages, implicating endolysosomal localization of TWIK-2 in inflammation 45,46.” This sentence is a bit misleading and should be clarified. From the references cited, it is movement of TWIK2 from the endolysosome to the plasma membrane that appears to be a critical step in the potassium efflux that mediates NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
We thank the reviewer for the correction. We have now replaced the sentence with “Translocation of TWIK-2 from endosome to plasma membrane is implicated in NLRP3-mediated inflammasome activation in macrophages, with Kcnk6 knockouts showing a suppressed inflammasome activation”.
2. - In figure 1 (and for nearly all electrophysiological traces shown in the manuscript), recording traces are shown on a signal scale that reads “Normalized I”. It is unclear what the non-transfected cells traces are normalized to? For clarity throughout the manuscript, it would be helpful if the authors explicitly discuss whether normalization was applied using a universal metric (which could be described in the methods section of the manuscript) or ad hoc for each set of recordings (in which case this should be described in each figure legends)
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue related to the normalization of electrophysiological traces. In the revised manuscript, all figures now display traces showing actual absolute current values instead of normalized signals. This update allows for direct comparison of current amplitudes across wild-type and mutant channels as well as non-transfected controls. Additionally, we now include current density for each experimental condition where appropriate, ensuring that differences in current amplitudes are not influenced by variations in cell size. We believe these revisions significantly improve the clarity and transparency of our data presentation and address the reviewer’s concern about normalization.
3- Given that the C-terminally truncated TWIK construct was not used for structure of detailed functional studies, this data could be omitted or moved to the methods section.
We agree with this reviewer’s observation that the data on C-terminally truncated TWIK-2 is not informative, beyond suggesting that TWIK-2 devoid of C-terminus is unstable compared to WT. In accordance, we have now removed the C-term truncation data of TWIK-2 from the revised manuscript.
4 - Is it meaningful that the loop region between V75-P89 is unresolved in the cryo-EM structure? In all other K2P structures, this loop is well resolved. Does this mean that the V75-P89 is dynamic in TWIK2, suggestive of a functional role? Or is this just a limitation of the resolutions of this TWIK2 structure compared to other K2P structures? Does 3D variability analysis in cryosparc give any indication of what is going on in this loop region?
The loop V75-P89 is a part of the CH2-PH1 region that harbors two predicted glycosylation sites, N79 and N85. We used HEK293 GnTI- cells, which lack N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase I activity, for overexpression of TWIK-2. So, it is likely that glycosylation at these sites is essential for stabilizing this loop, and without such glycosylation, this loop is flexible and hence poorly resolved in the cryo-EM density map. Interestingly, TWIK-2 structures reported by a different group recently also lacked this region 8. Despite using glycosylation-competent Expi293F cells and achieving an overall higher resolution structure (~2.9 Å). Perhaps, in TWIK-2 this loop is more dynamic than other K2Ps. Another group reported structures of TWIK-2 while this manuscript was under revision 7. They too use glycosylation-capable Expi293F cells as Khanra et. al., but were able to resolve the V75-P89 region in their cryo-EM map. Moreover, they find that amino acids 75-80 in this loop actually form a short helix called ‘ear helix’ that is unique to TWIK-2, proposed to stabilize the TWIK-2 cap domain. As this loop region can also potentially interact with the keystone inhibitor site and the K2P modulator pocket, we attempted to resolve this region using 3DVA and subsequent classification in cryoSPARC (Response Fig. 3). However, our attempts were not successful.
5- The panel in Figure 3 showing the relative locations of T106, T214, M135, and Y111 is critically important for understanding the orientation and relevance of these residues. I would suggest reworking this figure to make it clearer. The inset boxes are distracting, as each one has a different orientation relative to the main panel. Perhaps a clearly labeled “top view” showing the Y111 residues, “bottom view" showing the M135 residues, and a side view like shown in the left side of Figure 3A would be sufficient for this.
We have modified the figure as per the reviewer’s suggestions.
- “Notably, TWIK-2 channels elicited outward potassium currents that increased with depolarization (over +30 mV), suggesting voltage-dependent activation of TWIK-2” Isn’t this a surprising result, given that prior recordings in symmetrical potassium have shown inward rectification rather than outward rectification? Is there any methodologic explanation for this difference in observed functional behavior?
While it may seem surprising at first, the voltage-dependent activation of TWIK-2 seen in our recordings agrees with previous studies, especially those indicating that TWIK-2 is one of the least inwardly rectifying members of the K2P family, that inactivates and has a potential role in electrogenesis9–12. Compared to strongly rectifying K2P channels, such as TREK-1 or TASK-3, TWIK-2 exhibits more linear or even outwardly biased I–V relationships under certain recording conditions. Moreover, differences in rectification behavior—particularly outward currents at depolarized potentials—can depend on the expression system (e.g., Xenopus oocytes versus mammalian cells), ionic composition, and intracellular environment (e.g., Mg²⁺, polyamines, or pH). In our experiments, outward currents at voltages above +30 mV are probably caused by a combination of weak inherent rectification and the electrochemical driving force for K⁺ efflux under symmetrical or nearly symmetrical K⁺ conditions, rather than unusual voltage-dependent gating. To clarify this, we added a section in the discussion explaining how our findings align with the known electrophysiological properties of TWIK-2 and reflect system-dependent variability rather than an unexpected gating mechanism.
Response Figure 3: 3D variability analysis (3DVA) and subsequent classification to resolve V75-P89 loop. The region shaded in gray is a part of the supplementary figure 3 in the manuscript and has been included here only for reference. Particles from the best cluster displaying all the features of TWIK-2 from 3DVA step was used to generate an ab initio initial reference (cyan box). Next, particles from all clusters with robust cap domain features (red boxes) from the 3DVA step were pooled for clean up by heterogenous refinement and ab initio jobs. The final map obtained after NU-refinement, using the ab-initio reference generated from the best 3DVA cluster, resulted in a map with features and resolution that resembled the map already presented in the manuscript.
- Reference 70 in the manuscript includes data that describe the effect of mutations at the S4 site threonines in K2Ps. For nearly all K2Ps, these S4 site mutations cause a loss of voltage dependance. It is therefore interesting that in TWIK2, the T106A and T214A mutants maintain their voltage dependent gating. Is there any rationale for why this might be the case?
The reference 70 reports that in channels without a dedicated voltage-sensing domain, the SF itself acts as a gate and sensor. They demonstrate that mutating the conserved threonines at the SF to cysteines causes loss of voltage-dependent behavior. However, they also show that in addition to just these mutations, voltage-dependent behavior is also regulated by other factors such as mechanical force, ligands, and lipids13. Regulation of voltage-dependency of K2P channels by these auxiliary factors, apart from the residues at SF, has been shown in several K2P channels, especially the TREK family14–18. These reports suggest that the same K2P channel can switch between voltage-dependent and voltage-independent current responses depending on their conditions, perhaps a regulatory mechanism of certain K2P channels. T106A and T214A mutants display a reduced-voltage dependency in our experiments, but not a complete loss of voltage-dependency. Because we see that the central cavity is occupied by lipid-like densities in our cryo-EM map, and because TWIK-2 has an ability to translocate between endosomes and plasma membrane and has been proposed to interact with other proteins via its C-terminus, we believe it is possible that voltage-dependency in TWIK-2 could be a context dependent phenomenon, in addition to being regulated by the residues at the SF. However, identification of all the factors in TWIK-2 that regulate its channel activity needs furthermore substantial efforts.
- “Mutations T106A and T214A disturb these networks of hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions that stabilize the base of the SF and make the channel less selective and more open (Figure 3B-3F).” The functional experiments presented in this section use only a single ionic composition and are not suited to adequately address ion selectivity. Please support with data or omit this claim.
We agree with the reviewer that with only a single ionic composition, it is hard to address the ion selectivity of TWIK-2. We have rephrased this statement and added the observations from T106A and T214A double mutants’ whole cell recordings to this section. We find that the double mutants display greater current density compared to single mutants and wild-type TWIK-2.
- Is the TWIK2 Y111H mutant pH sensitive like the TWIK1 channel? This seems like an obvious experiment to try and would be informative to understanding differences between TWIK1 and TWIK2 functions.
As already discovered by a few groups, H122 in TWIK-1 and H98 in TASK-3 although regarded as major proton-sensing amino acids in the SF1-M2 loop, are not the only determinants of pH sensitivity in K2P channels4,19–22. While the Y111H mutant of TWIK-2 is a TWIK-1-like mutation, we did not anticipate that it would single-handedly change the pH sensitivity of TWIK-2. In the revised version of the manuscript, we show that the pH dependency of channel activation and activity of Y111H TWIK-2 is the same as that of wild-type like TWIK-2. Furthermore, we observe that in our assay setup, TWIK-1 showed pH-dependent current changes, albeit mild. These observations have been included in the revised version of the manuscript in a separate figure, and the corresponding text has been modified accordingly.
- More methodological detail of the automated patch clamp technique would be helpful to understand the experimental system. Are drugs applied to the intracellular face of the channel (via syncropatch pipette) or extracellular via bath?
We appreciate the reviewer's request for clarification regarding the delivery of compounds in the automated patch clamp system. To address this, we have expanded the Methods section to include more detailed information about the experimental setup. Unless otherwise noted, all compounds were applied extracellularly using an external addition protocol, following the standard procedures for the SyncroPatch system. The SyncroPatch features a high-speed, multi-channel pipetting robot that manages all liquid additions and removals during the experiments. This robot can simultaneously add various external compounds—such as drugs, ligands, and chemicals—to each of the 384 wells, enabling a large number of experiments to be conducted simultaneously. Additionally, the robot performs quick and efficient solution exchanges in the wells. Although the system permits compound delivery to the intracellular face via an intracellular exchange solution, this study only examined the external application of pharmacological agents to aid in easier application, better ability to perform cumulative concentration-response curves, and for clear pre- and post-drug comparisons. This clarification has been added to the ‘Automated patch clamp recordings’ section within the Materials and Methods, to improve reproducibility and transparency in our data interpretation.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
“The manuscript of Ma et al, provides new insights into the modulation of the K2P channel TWIK-2 using structural and electrophysiological data. The study provides the first cryo-EM structure of the full-length TWIK-2 at 3.7Å resolution, which is accompanied by mutagenesis studies and the use of a whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology workflow. The authors show that TWIK-2 is pH-insensitive but slightly voltage-gated and suggest potential different binding modes or mechanisms of inhibition in TWIK-2 for two of the four tested K2P modulators (ML365 and NPBA).
The work is well executed and well written. However, overall the study fall a bit short. The new insights provided do not represent a big step forward in improving our understanding of how TWIK-2 (and K2P channels in general) function and are regulated. The substance and depth of the study could be/have been strengthened by more structure-guided mutagenesis studies, a more robust comparison of their new automated electrophysiology setup, a better literature comparison with (mutagenesis studies of) TWIK-1 and other K2P channels, or even more structural data or structural analysis. While I understand that addressing them all might be out of the scope of this study, the manuscript requires a bit more of depth. Specific suggestion would be (major comments):”
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions to increase the depth of our work. We have revised the manuscript accordingly and addressed the changes point-by-point in our response below.
1. In total ‘only’ four residues are identified as different/interesting and tested. Namely M135A, T106A, T214A and Y111H. What about other positions, e.g., around the cavity or along the ion conductance pathway? Is everything else conserved? What about testing mutating the same sites with other substitutes or using double and triple mutations to gain more insights? Compare in more depth with TWIK-1 and other K2P channels.
We agree with the reviewer that the mutant selection was sparse. To address this, we have included 4 more single mutants in the revised version of the manuscript, focusing on the regions around the SF (S213A and Y111A), the K2P modulator pocket (F98A), and hydrophobic cuff (M135N). Additionally, we also tested the effect of the T106A/T214A double mutant on TWIK-2 channel activity. We have also included an extensive comparison of TWIK-2 and TWIK-1, especially the channel activity, inhibition, and differences in the structure. Lastly, we have reformatted the existing comparison with other K2P channels to make it more apparent. Please see the remaining rebuttal, the results, and the discussion sections for more details.
2. Most striking in this endeavor is the mutant Y111H. The authors show that in contrast to TWIK-1, TWIK-2 is pH-insensitive, with the histidine in that position being the pH-sensing residue in TWIK-1. While the authors go on and attempt to describe some of the differences observed for TWIK-2-Y111H, they never actually tested if this mutant has become pH-sensitive. Considering the overall conservation between TWIK-1 and TWIK-2 this would be expected and highly interesting to test. Further, to test the importance of the tyrosine and decouple it from a pH sensor position, a mutation to another residue, e.g. Y111A and Y111L would be interesting. Finally, the fact that TWIK-2_Y111H mutant carries the pH sensor of TWIK-1 must be mentioned in all clarity also in the results and discussion section and taking into account during interpretation.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of Y111H. H122 in TWIK-1, although regarded as a major proton-sensing amino acid in the SF1-M2 loop, is not the only determinant of pH4,20,22. While the Y111H mutant of TWIK-2 is a TWIK-1-like mutation, we did not anticipate that it would single-handedly change the pH sensitivity of TWIK-2. In the revised version of the manuscript, as per the reviewer’s suggestion, we also compare the pH-dependency of TWIK-1 in our assay setup and test the effect of the TWIK-1-like Y111H mutant on the pH-dependence of TWIK-2 channel activity. We find that TWIK-1 is pH-dependent while TWIK-2 is not, despite the introduction of TWIK-1 like Y111H mutation. As per the reviewer’s suggestion, we also tested the effect of changing the bulky Y111 to a smaller aliphatic amino acid as alanine, on TWIK-2 channel activity. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition. Perhaps, to speculate, the role of Y111 in TWIK-2 is maintaining the SF1-M2 loop integrity to facilitate allosteric coupling between the bottom and top of the SF.
3. I appreciate and highly welcome the high-throughput patch clamp workflow presented by the authors. However, considering i) the discrepancies mentioned by the authors on electrophysiology studies for TWIK-2 in the literature, and ii) the mentioned inconsistencies between some of their electrophysiology data with that published before, the authors should do a more thorough comparison. If possible, between methods conducted by themselves with the same non-glycosylated constructs (conventional patch clamp and high-throughput patch clamp). But perhaps more importantly, use TWIK-1 in their automated whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology setup, for which more robust recordings have been reported. This would allow us to assess and compare TWIK-1 and TWIK-2 and the different workflows better.
We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. While we agree that not all experiments performed using conventional patch clamp can be adopted to a high-throughput automated patch clamp approach, screening of inhibitors and testing the relative change in channel activity upon mutagenesis has been reliably demonstrated by several groups. As there are already reports that compare high-throughput APC with conventional patch clamp techniques23–25, we prioritized to compare between TWIK-1 and TWIK-2. Using the same expression construct background and Syncropatch assay set up, we found that the overall TWIK-1 currents are comparable to TWIK-2. However, we notice that TWIK-1, unlike TWIK-2, shows pH dependency, albeit only mild. We also find that TWIK-1 is faster activating than TWIK-2 and is more susceptible to inhibition by ML365 and NPBA compared to TWIK-2. In addition to the comparison of electrophysiological properties of TWIK-2 and TWIK-1, in the revised version of the manuscript, we also include a detailed structure comparison at the end of the results section.
4. The slightly different impact found for two of the tested inhibitors makes the discussion a bit ambiguous as to their potential different binding mode. I wonder if an attempt to solve an inhibitor-bound structure would be in the scope of this study as the authors seem to be able to obtain enough stable protein and the processing appears rather straightforward.
We agree with the reviewer that the structures of TWIK-2 with ML365 and NPBA could provide more information about their mechanism of binding. We collected and analyzed cryo-EM datasets of TWIK-2 with ML365 or NPBA. We observed that in the presence of these ligands, the sample appeared to be more heterogeneous, resulting in maps of lower quality compared to the apo TWIK-2 map reported in this manuscript. The resolutions of both the inhibitor-bound TWIK-2 maps are fairly similar, with one common feature being the loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities that we observed in apo-TWIK-2 near the hydrophobic cuff. Of course, it is possible that loss of tubular lipid-like densities is a factor of poor resolution of the map. To make reasonable comparisons, we filtered the apo-TWIK-2 map to ~4Å (Response Fig. 1 above in page 2 of this document).
While we do not see any additional non-protein density in the ML365 dataset, we do observe some non-protein density immediately below the SF in the case of the NPBA dataset. The non-protein density that we see in the NPBA dataset is not seen in the apo TWIK-2; however, the poor resolution of the map, and the size and shape of the density, preclude us from modeling NPBA at this site. Hence, we have not included these efforts in the manuscript and are presenting them here in the rebuttal. As the efforts to obtain high-resolution inhibitor-bound structures were not fruitful, we employed site-directed mutagenesis to identify a potential NPBA binding site by performing more mutations in the SF, K2P modulator pocket, and around the hydrophobic cuff. We have discussed these in the main manuscript, and our findings suggest that the potential binding site for NPBA, as hinted by additional density in the map, could be below the SF. The mutagenesis exploration still does not identify the site for ML365 unambiguously. However, loss of strong tubular lipid-like densities around the hydrophobic cuff compared to apo TWIK-2 makes us suspect that ML365, like NPBA could bind through the cavity, albeit interacting with different residues compared to NPBA.

Can the authors comment on the following: With regards to the processing of the cryo-EM data, I wonder if the authors also tested refining the other 3 classes obtained before proceeding with a final NU-refinement of one of the classes. Considering the authors interpret their structure as an intermediate conductive state, I wonder if there were some hints at other conformational states captured in the data.
We tried refining the other 3 classes shown in the penultimate step of data processing pipeline, but the resultant refined maps from these classes were of poor quality and offered no additional new information. Hence, we went ahead with the map denoted as “class 0” for final refinement and model building (Response Fig. 4)
Response Figure 4: NU-refinements of all the classes post 3D classification.
6. Could the authors comment why they mutated Y111H to mimic the corresponding TWIK-1 residue, but then mutated M135A instead of M135L (which would be the corresponding TWIK-1 residue)? What was the rationale/strategy here? And here again, it would have been ideal to have TWIK-1 as a control experiment, and to compare Y111H with.
Methionine, leucine, and alanine are all hydrophobic nonpolar amino acids. Between M135L and M135A, the alanine substitution of methionine reduces the size of the side chain drastically affecting not only the size of the pocket near M135 but also affecting the relative hydrophobic surface area. As we saw lipid-like densities around M135 amino acid, suspecting their role in regulation of channel activity, we anticipated M135A mutation to have drastic effect on TWIK-2 activity compared to M135L. In the revised version of the manuscript, we also tested M135N to explore the role of introduction of polar amino acid in this region on TWIK-2 activity. We notice that both M135A and M135N mutants exhibit slightly slower channel activation and show no drastic effect on the channel activity. However, M135A shows a greater loss of NPBA inhibition compared to M135N suggesting that removing the bulky amino acid at this position affects the efficacy of NPBA. Similarly, we also tested the effect of changing the pocket around Y111 on TWIK-2 channel activity using a Y111A mutant. We found that Y111A was slow deactivating while Y111H was slow activating, compared to wild-type, like TWIK-2. Both of these mutations caused a loss of NPBA-mediated inhibition. In the revised version of the manuscript, as per the reviewer’s suggestion, we also compare pH-dependency of TWIK-1 in our assay set up and test the effect of TWIK-1 like Y111H mutant on the pH-dependence of TWIK-2 channel activity. We find that TWIK-1 is pH-dependent while TWIK-2 is not, despite the introduction of TWIK-1 like Y111H mutation.
7. Could the authors comment/expand on the voltage-dependence of TWIK-2 in the, and whether other K2P channels have also been found to be so.
In a 2016 study Schewe et al. provided significant insights into the voltage-dependent gating mechanisms of K2P channel, challenging the traditional view that voltage-sensing channel requires a canonical voltage-sensing domain. Instead, they proposed the SF to have a “check valve” gating behavior. They also note that this type of voltage-dependency has been observed in most K2Ps except TWIK113. Apart from the residues at the SF, voltage-dependent behavior in K2Ps, especially the TREK family, is also regulated by other factors such as mechanical force, ligands, and lipids 14–18. These reports suggest that the same K2P channel can switch between voltage-dependent and voltage-independent current responses depending on their conditions, perhaps a regulatory mechanism of certain K2P channels. Because we see that the central cavity is occupied by lipid-like densities in our cryo-EM map, and because TWIK-2 has an ability to translocate between endosomes and plasma membrane and has been proposed to interact with other proteins via its C-terminus, we believe it is possible that voltage-dependency in TWIK-2 could be a context dependent phenomenon.
8. While I appreciate the modeling of potential lipids and co for the interpretation and figure rendering of non-protein densities, considering the high ambiguity, I expect that the authors have no intention of including it in the to be deposited model. (in the era of AlphaFold and machine learning, everything that is deposited can and will be use by AI or others)
Compared to other K2Ps, the extra non-protein densities of TWIK-2 are a unique feature and may be endogenous molecules involved in channel regulation. As noted in the manuscript, we have not verified the exact nature of these lipid-like molecules, and hence we have modeled hydrocarbon tails in these densities. While this manuscript was under revision, two other groups reported structures of TWIK-2, and both groups observed tubular “non-protein” densities, especially in the fenestration site and in the central cavity 7,8. The former modeled acyl chains in the fenestration sites, while in the latter manuscript, the authors modeled lipids in these densities and proposed a mechanism of lipid-mediated regulation of TWIK-2 channel activity. Encouraged by multiple groups, independently, discovering lipid-like tubular densities in TWIK-2, we have decided to deposit the model with hydrocarbon chains modeled into these densities.

- Figure S3: FSC curves indicates the mask during refinement is too tight and could be optimized
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. However, the unique architecture of K2P channels allows detergent micelles to occupy grooves formed between various secondary structure elements in the transmembrane region. Moreover, the detergent that we used for purification is DMNG. Neopentyl glycol class of detergents has low CMCs and are known to form heterogeneous micelles with varying sizes depending on the effective concentration of the detergent 27. To avoid heterogeneity in micelle size and stochastic detergent densities from interfering with refinement, we had to use a relatively tight mask to reconstruct a map with interpretable features at the protein-micelle interface. We have tried to dilate the mask more, and the resulting structure could not reach as high a resolution as the current map. A relatively tight mask is needed to effectively remove the micelle density that is tightly bound to our protein.
